sens: Containing water, which is moist
Fresh and full of sap, referring to wood
Alive and vigorous, referring to a person
G5200.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is wet or moist, as opposed to dry. It conveys the idea of freshness and humidity.
2. When applied to wood, it refers to green wood, that which has just been cut and is still full of sap, in contrast to dry and dead wood. In Luke 23:31, Jesus says: "If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen to the dry?" — he speaks of fresh and living wood to evoke his own strength and life.
3. By extension, the word can qualify a living and healthy person, full of vigor, while dry wood represents weakness or death.
G5200.origine: The Greek word hugros comes from a root meaning "to flow" or "to run out." Its basic image is that of moisture and water. In Hebrew, in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often renders the word lakh (לַח), which means precisely "moist" or "fresh." It is a word that naturally evokes life and freshness, in contrast to dryness which symbolizes death or exhaustion.
G5200.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 23:31, where Jesus uses it in a parable addressed to the women who weep as he follows him to the cross. He contrasts green wood with dry wood to express an idea: if one treats harshly the one who is alive and strong, what will be done to the one who is weak and dead? This image speaks of Jesus himself as the green wood (living and powerful) and his people as the dry wood (destined for condemnation). The context is that of the Passion, where God's justice is exercised on the just before striking the guilty.
G5200.portee: This word from Jesus reminds us that if the just suffers, it is for our salvation. By accepting the cross while he is "green," that is, alive and innocent, Jesus intercedes for us who are "dry," that is, dead in our sins. It invites every believer to see in the suffering of Christ a divine justice that first acts on the innocent to spare the guilty.

sens: Stone or ceramic container, intended to hold and transport liquids such as water or wine
Pot or urn of various shapes, used to store or preserve various substances
G5201.detail:
1. It is primarily a water pot, a vessel intended to hold water. The six stone jars mentioned in John 2:6 at Cana were specifically used for the ritual washings of the Jews: they were practical, sturdy containers, each holding about two or three measures (approximately 20 to 30 liters). It is in these jars that Jesus orders the servants to fill with water (John 2:7), before turning that water into wine.
2. More broadly, the word designates any pottery or stone container — pot, urn, jug — intended to hold various things: water, wine, oil, silver, etc. The Samaritan woman in John 4:28 goes to draw water with her jug, an everyday object that she hastily leaves behind to go announce the good news. The word encompasses all these domestic and ritual uses.
G5201.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means what contains water (from ὕδωρ, "water"). It is a common word in classical Greek and New Testament Greek to designate any container or vessel intended to hold liquids or other substances. The word appears mainly in the Gospels, where it evokes daily life and the simple gestures of home.
G5201.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospel of John. John 2:6-7 recounts the stone jars used at the wedding at Cana: these are containers related to Jewish worship and ritual purity, and it is in them that Jesus performs his first miracle. John 4:28 mentions the Samaritan woman's jug, a mundane object of daily life, symbolizing her ordinary life that she abandons to follow Christ. Everywhere, the word designates a domestic or ritual utensil, very concrete and deeply rooted in the habits of the time.
G5201.portee: This simple word reminds us that the Gospel speaks of real things and places: stone jars, a jug, the well, water. It is in these ordinary gestures — filling with water, drawing, abandoning an object — that great spiritual turning points manifest: the first sign of Jesus at Cana, the conversion of the Samaritan woman. Our everyday life, with its humble objects, is not exempt from the presence and action of God.

sens: To drink water as the sole or main beverage
To abstain from wine and other alcoholic drinks
G5202.detail:
1. The word designates the action of drinking water, understood as the ordinary and sober drink. It is a simple and daily act, that of someone who consumes only water to quench their thirst. In 1 Timothy 5:23, Paul speaks of someone who "drinks only water," which characterizes a very strict and wine-free diet.
2. The word also carries the idea of a practice of abstinence or voluntary sobriety: drinking only water means refraining from wine and fermented drinks. It is a choice of temperance or, in some cases, of mortification. The context in 1 Timothy 5:23 suggests that such a dietary restriction is not advisable for health.
G5202.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: "ὕδωρ" (hydôr, water) and "πίνω" (pinô, to drink). It literally means "to drink water." In Hebrew, the parallel idea is rendered by "שָׁתָה מַיִם" (shata mayim, to drink waters). The verb describes an ordinary and concrete practice, without intrinsic moral connotation, but which in the Pauline context takes on a sense of discipline or austerity.
G5202.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 5:23. Paul uses it to advise Timothy not to persist in a strict abstinence from wine, as it affects his fragile health. The context suggests that Timothy had adopted a rigorous practice of drinking only water, likely out of concern for purity or spiritual discipline. Paul does not condemn wine in itself; he acknowledges that alcoholic beverages can have legitimate and beneficial uses.
G5202.portee: This passage teaches that strict and systematic abstinence is not a Christian ideal to impose without discernment. Paul values the health of the body and practical wisdom: it is better to adapt to one's physical constitution than to follow rigid rules that may be harmful. It is a call to reasoned freedom and self-love in permissible matters.

sens: Affected by an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body
G5203.detail: 1. Dropsical refers to a person suffering from a condition where the body accumulates too much fluid, causing visible swelling. It is a medical condition that makes the patient heavy and fatigued (Luke 14:2: "a dropsical man was in front of him").
G5203.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek "hydro" meaning water, and "opsis" meaning appearance or state. The Greek word "hydropikos" literally describes someone who has the appearance swollen by water accumulated in their body. It is a disease known since antiquity, often related to liver or heart problems.
G5203.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:2. Jesus is in the house of a chief Pharisee on the Sabbath, and this dropsical man is present. This incident immediately precedes the miraculous healing of this man, highlighting the contrast between visible physical illness and Jesus' power to restore the body.
G5203.portee: This unique mention of a dropsical disease in the Gospel illustrates how Jesus does not overlook the needs of the body. Even in a hostile context (a meal at a Pharisee's house), he sees the suffering and heals it, showing that compassion for the sick is more important than human rules. It reminds the reader that healing is about restoring the whole person.

sens: Colorless, odorless liquid essential for life
Element used for baptism and purification
Rivers, streams, seas, and all bodies of water
Biblical image of divine truth, grace, and salvation
G5204.detail:
1. Water is the liquid that quenches thirst and covers a large part of creation (Matthew 14:28-29, where the disciples walk on water; Revelation 1:15, where it is described as a sound like many waters). It evokes life and renewal.

2. In the Bible, water becomes the sign of baptism and moral and spiritual purification. Jesus was baptized in water (Matthew 3:16), and baptism symbolizes the renewal and transformation of the heart. Ephesians 5:26 speaks of the baptism of water as a means of sanctification.

3. Water also refers to natural bodies of water: rivers, springs, seas. Revelation 8:10 describes a star falling on the rivers and springs of water, evoking cosmic events.

4. Spiritually, Jesus calls living water the image of eternal life and divine grace (John 4:10-11: "the living water"). It is an image of what truly quenches the soul and satisfies it forever.
G5204.origine: The Greek word ὕδωρ (hudōr) is one of the oldest in the Indo-European vocabulary and literally means "that which flows." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew מַיִם (mayim). The word belongs to the same family as the French "hydro-" (water). The starting image is that of liquid flowing, which reflects the very nature of water.
G5204.emploi: The word appears about 70 times in the New Testament, mainly in contexts of narrative events (Matthew and Mark) and theological teachings (John and Revelation). It is very concrete at the beginning of the Gospels: baptismal water (Matthew 3:11), water serving daily needs (Mark 14:13, woman with the pitcher), miraculous water and food (John 2:9, water turned into wine; John 5:4, pool). In John, the word gradually shifts towards spiritual meaning: living water becomes a symbol of grace and salvation (John 4:10-14; Revelation 21:6; 22:17). The contrast between earthly water that does not satisfy and living water that quenches forever reinforces this symbolic significance.
G5204.portee: For the reader, water reminds us that Jesus gives true life and ultimate spiritual satisfaction. Baptism marks the entry into a relationship with God through the renewal of the heart. The image of living water invites us to drink from the very source of divine grace, not from earthly substitutes that leave us empty. It is an invitation to transformation and satisfaction that only Christ can provide.

sens: water that falls from the sky in drops
act or process of raining
sign of God's blessing on the earth
that which fertilizes the earth and makes it fruitful
manifestation of divine power
G5205.detail: 1. Rain is the water that falls from the sky in drops. It is the concrete meteorological phenomenon: in Acts 28:2, rain falls with cold, preventing the shipwrecked from progressing. 2. The word also refers to the act of raining, the event itself: in Revelation 11:6, the two prophets have the power to shut the sky so that no rain falls. 3. In the Bible, rain is often the visible sign of God's blessing on His people. In Acts 14:17, God bears witness to Himself by sending rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, thus showing His goodness. 4. Rain fertilizes and gives life to the earth: in Hebrews 6:7, a land watered by rain produces useful herbs. It is the vital element for the harvest. 5. It also symbolizes God's sovereign power over creation: in James 5:18, after Elijah's prayer, the sky gives rain and the earth produces its fruit, showing that God answers prayers and controls all natural elements.
G5205.origine: The Greek word huetos comes from the verb "to rain." It is a simple and common word that paints the image of water falling from the sky. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, equivalent words are used to describe both natural rain and rain as a divine gift. Rain is a key element throughout Scripture: it nourishes the people, rewards obedience, and can also be withheld as punishment.
G5205.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, in James, and in Revelation. It is always concrete but rarely neutral: rain is either a manifestation of divine generosity (Acts 14:17), or a physical obstacle (Acts 28:2), or a necessary creative force (Hebrews 6:7, James 5:7, 5:18), or a phenomenon subject to prophetic will (Revelation 11:6). James 5:7 introduces the poetic notion of the "early and latter rains," agricultural cycles by which God sustains life. The word never has a figurative or strictly spiritual meaning: it remains attached to real rain, but this real rain is always loaded with theological significance.
G5205.portee: Rain reminds the believer that their life depends entirely on divine providence. It teaches patience (James 5:7: the farmer waits for the rain) and trust in God who provides what is necessary. It also shows that prayer has real power: Elijah prayed, and rain came, thus fulfilling God's will. Finally, rain invites us to recognize that every good gift comes from God and should be received with gratitude.

sens: Legal and familial act by which someone is taken as a son or daughter
Relationship established by God with Israel in the Old Covenant
Relationship established by God with believers in Jesus Christ
State of one who becomes a child of God through faith
Final transformation of the bodies of the redeemed
Cry of the heart of the child towards his Father
G5206.detail:
1. Adoption is the act by which someone is brought into a family as a son or daughter, even though they are not related by blood. It was a well-known legal practice in the Greek and Roman world, granting the adopted person all the rights and status of a child born in the household.
2. God established a relationship of adoption with Israel: the people of Israel were chosen and raised by God as His children, receiving glory, the covenant, and the law (Romans 9:4). This is a unique and inexhaustible privilege.
3. Christians — those who believe in Jesus Christ — have become children of God by adoption. Ephesians 1:5 states that God predestined us to be His adopted children through Jesus Christ.
4. This adoption is not merely a legal status: it is a living and personal relationship. The believer can cry out "Abba! Father!" — a tender and childlike term — because the Spirit testifies that he has truly become a child of God (Romans 8:15).
5. Adoption will reach its perfection when the bodies of believers are redeemed and transformed: this is what Paul calls adoption in its final sense, the complete redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23).
6. The word expresses not only a status but a cry of the heart: the believer, having become a child of God, can address Him with the confidence and tenderness of a small child towards his father.
G5206.origine: The Greek word υἱοθεσία (uhiothesia) comes from υἱός (huios), "son," and θέσις (thesis), "action of placing" — literally "placing as a son." This foundational image (placing someone in the position of a son) became a legal term in Greek and Roman law to denote legal adoption. Paul borrows this word from secular language to express the relationship of God with Israel and with believers: a relationship that is not natural (one is not born a child of God by blood), but established and confirmed by the sovereign will of God.
G5206.emploi: The word "adoption" appears five times in the New Testament, and all occurrences are found in Paul (Romans 8:15, 8:23, 9:4; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:5). Paul uses it to describe two complementary realities: first, the adoption of Israel by God in the Old Covenant (Romans 9:4), which is a historical fact and evidence of God's sovereign choice. Then, and most importantly, the adoption of Christians by God in Jesus Christ (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:5), which is the result of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Paul emphasizes that it is accomplished progressively: first received by faith and the Spirit (Romans 8:15), it will be completed when our bodies are redeemed (Romans 8:23). It is a gift of grace, never earned, always desired by God in His love.
G5206.portee: This word transforms the spiritual life of the believer. It shows that the relationship with God is not that of a fearful servant before his master, but that of a beloved child before his father: God has chosen us as His children (Ephesians 1:5). It gives the believer assurance: possessing the Spirit, he can cry "Abba! Father!" with the confidence of a child (Romans 8:15). Finally, it opens hope: our adoption is not yet complete; it will be fulfilled when our bodies are transformed and redeemed (Romans 8:23), reminding us that our inheritance is only partially realized on earth.

sens: male child of a father and mother
descendant, heir of a family or lineage
one who belongs to a group or participates in a quality
disciple or follower of a master or doctrine
Jesus, the Son of God in a unique and eternal sense
Jesus clothed in His human nature and His role as judge
G5207.detail:
1. In the ordinary sense: a son is the male child born of a father; it is the natural bond of filiation. In Matthew 1:1, we read "the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham," where the sons are the direct descendants who inherit the name and the promise.
2. In a broader sense, the term designates the heir of a family or a royal line. In Matthew 22:2, the king makes a wedding feast for his son, who will receive the kingdom. It can also mean descendants in a collective sense: "the sons of Israel" for the entire people (Matthew 27:9).
3. Even more broadly, the word expresses belonging or participation in a quality: a "son of the evil one" (Matthew 13:38) is someone who belongs to the evil one and acts like him; a "son of light" (Luke 16:8) is one who lives in the light and shares its nature.
4. Applied to humans in relation to God: the "sons of God" are those who participate in the divine nature and eternal life, as in Matthew 5:9 (the peacemakers are "sons of God"). It is an adoption, a spiritual transformation.
5. In its unique and incomparable sense: Jesus is "the Son of God" in an eternal and singular way, not by creation but by His own nature. In Mark 15:39, the centurion confesses: "Truly, this man was the Son of God." 
6. "The Son of Man" is a title that Jesus applies to Himself to emphasize both His real humanity (He is truly a man) and His role as the universal judge who came from heaven. In John 12:34, the crowd asks: "Who is this Son of Man?"
G5207.origine: The Greek word υἱός comes from an Indo-European root simply meaning male child. In Hebrew and Aramaic, the equivalent בֵּן (ben) or בַּר (bar) is used in the same way, both literally and figuratively (a man belonging to a group, a quality, or an era). The Aramaic expression "son of man" (בַּר אנשׁ), derived from Daniel 7:13, has profoundly influenced the usage in the New Testament. The word also maintains connections with concepts of spiritual filiation and inheritance throughout the biblical context.
G5207.emploi: The word υἱός appears 348 times in the New Testament (368 in French in the Segond). It is omnipresent in the four Gospels and the Epistles. In the ordinary sense, it denotes the father-son relationship in genealogies and family narratives (Matthew 1:1; Galatians 4:30). In a very frequent metaphorical sense, it expresses belonging to a moral or spiritual reality: "son of the evil one" (Matthew 13:38), "son of light" (Luke 16:8), "son of peace" (Luke 10:6). The phrase "Son of God" applied to Jesus holds central importance (Mark 15:39; Matthew 16:16) and denotes His divinity and eternal status with the Father. The expression "Son of Man," used exclusively by Jesus Himself except in Acts 7:56, emphasizes His true humanity and His authority as the final judge (John 12:34; Matthew 24:27-30). The context thus transforms the meaning of the simple genealogical term into a theological affirmation.
G5207.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals the dual nature of Christ: true God (Son of God) and true man (Son of Man), as well as His unique role as Savior and judge. It also shows that believers become in turn "sons of God" by grace, heirs with Christ of the eternal promise. Understanding the richness of this term helps the believer grasp the incarnation and his own adoption into the family of God.

sens: A collection of trees covering a large area of land
Wood, material of wood
Raw material, substance from which things are made
G5208.detail:
1. A forest is a vast area covered with trees, the wooded landscape. This is the most common meaning of the word in nature. James 3:5 uses it to evoke a large forest that catches fire: the image is that of an immense area of trees tightly packed together.
2. The word can also refer to the wood itself, the material from which trees are made, or the cut wood used as fuel or material. It is wood as a resource, a raw material that is exploited.
3. In Greek thought, particularly among philosophers, the word shifts to an abstract meaning: it designates the raw material from which things are composed, in contrast to form or structure. It is the raw material of the universe.
G5208.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root that denotes the thickness and density of wood. In ancient Greek texts, it appears in Homer and historians to speak of forests and wood. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament translates terms like "succah" (thick bush) or "yawen" (forest) with this word, showing that it captures the idea of dense and extensive vegetation.
G5208.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:5, where the apostle uses it in a striking comparison: a small tongue is like a small fire capable of setting a large forest ablaze. The image evokes the immense destructive power of a small ignited thing — the uncontrolled tongue becomes a force of destruction capable of devastating, just as a small fire can reduce an entire forest to ashes. It is a call to vigilance over our words.
G5208.portee: This image of the forest catching fire reminds the reader of the dangerous power of words. Our words, even if they seem insignificant when taken in isolation, carry within them considerable destructive power. The image of the forest, a vast place rich in life, reduced to ashes, makes concrete and visceral the call to control our tongue and weigh our words wisely.

sens: A man who opposes sound Christian doctrine in the early churches
False teacher harming the faith of believers
G5211.detail: Hymenaeus is a character mentioned twice in the epistles to Timothy as representing a threat to the early Church. In 1 Timothy 1:20, Paul designates him as someone who has blasphemed and whom the apostle has "delivered to Satan" — a disciplinary measure to stop him in his destructive work. In 2 Timothy 2:17, he is named again alongside Philetus: together, they teach "things that are not proper," corrupting the faith of some with their false doctrines, particularly concerning the resurrection (as indicated by the context of 2 Timothy 2:18). Hymenaeus embodies the type of false teacher who, through his erroneous teaching and insolence towards holy truths, threatens the edifice of faith in Christian communities.
G5211.origine: The name "Hymenaeus" derives from the Greek Hymen, the god of the hymn and marriage among the Greeks. It was a name borne by men in the Greco-Roman world, here designating a specific individual who emerged as a figure of doctrinal opposition in the context of the churches to which Paul writes Timothy. The name has no Hebrew etymology or relation to the Old Testament.
G5211.emploi: Hymenaeus appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the pastoral epistles addressed to Timothy. In 1 Timothy 1:20, Paul mentions him among those who have blasphemed and whom he has handed over to the judgment of Satan, a serious church discipline. In 2 Timothy 2:17, the same character is associated with Philetus, both describing representatives of a specific heresy harming the community. These two occurrences make him a concrete example of a false teacher that church leaders must identify and counter. The context of 2 Timothy 2:18 reveals that their error concerned the resurrection, likely its denial or reinterpretation.
G5211.portee: The mention of Hymenaeus invites the Christian reader to remain vigilant against false teachings and doctrinal corruption that threaten the Church. His case illustrates the seriousness with which Paul and the early Church viewed the protection of the truth of the Gospel and the warning against those who stray from it. For a Christian community, it is a reminder that sound doctrine is not a secondary detail, but a central issue of faith life.

sens: To sing in honor of someone or something
To sing praises, hymns to God
To raise a melody of communal praise
To celebrate through song
G5214.detail:
1. The verb primarily means "to sing" in the literal sense of the word: to produce a melody with the voice. It is a natural musical and vocal act. When Jesus and his disciples "sang hymns" after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26), they are likely singing the Psalms of Hallel, the traditional hymns of the Jewish Passover.
2. In a biblical context, singing is never neutral: it almost always becomes an act of praise towards God. When Paul and Silas "sing praises to God" in prison, they are not merely humming; they express their faith and joy despite suffering (Acts 16:25).
3. Biblical singing is often communal: several voices unite to exalt God together. This is why the context of the assembly frequently returns — Jesus "sings" to the Father "in the midst of the assembly" (Hebrews 2:12), manifesting that this song unites the community.
4. This verb also carries the idea of solemn celebration and recognition: to sing is to acknowledge the greatness of the one being praised.
G5214.origine: The word comes from the noun "hymnos" (hymn), which in ancient Greece referred to a song of honor, a poetic composition in honor of a god or an illustrious person. In Hebrew, the biblical verb is rendered by several roots: "hallal" (to make noise, to praise, to celebrate), "shir" (to sing), or "yadah" (to give thanks). The Greek word emphasizes the musical and laudatory aspect of the gesture.
G5214.emploi: The verb "humneō" appears 4 times in the New Testament, almost always to speak of liturgical or devotional singing. Matthew and Mark report its use by Jesus during the Last Supper. Paul and Silas are the subjects in a context of prison and suffering, showing that this song expresses trust despite the trial. Hebrews uses it to describe the activity of the resurrected Christ who praises the Father in the assembly of the Church. In all cases, it is a cultic act, a mode of expression of faith in a communal context.
G5214.portee: This word invites the reader to see singing as an authentic expression of faith, not a superficial element of worship. Paul and Silas in prison show that praising God through song is a living response to His presence, even in the midst of suffering. Singing unites the Christian community around a common confession of divine greatness: this is why it remains central in the liturgy and prayer of the Church.

sens: A song of praise addressed to God
A religious song characterized by its content of divine celebration
A musical expression of faith and worship
G5215.detail:
1. A hymn is a song composed to praise and celebrate God. It is a sung text, often structured, that expresses gratitude, adoration, and joy towards the Lord. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, hymns are mentioned alongside psalms and spiritual songs as forms of praise that Christians should share with one another.
2. The hymn is distinguished from the psalm by its orientation: while the psalm is sung with musical accompaniment (the Greek word psalmós refers to the instrument), the hymn emphasizes the content of praise. Biblical hymns are words of celebration addressed directly to God for His glory and works.
G5215.origine: The Greek word humnos originally refers, in ancient Greek culture, to a festive song in honor of gods or heroes. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), it translates the Hebrew tehilla (praise), nigguina (musical song), and shir (song). The word has retained this religious meaning of a song of praise, but applied to God the Father and Jesus Christ in the New Testament. It is a word that unites the Greek tradition of honor songs with the Hebrew practice of praise.
G5215.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, only in the Pauline epistles. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, Paul lists the three forms of singing that should characterize the life of the Church: psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. These two passages are identical in structure, confirming that hymns are a central practice of early Christian worship. The hymn is associated with mutual exhortation and teaching, suggesting that hymns are not only an expression of emotion but also a pedagogical means of conveying faith. Hymns are sung "with all your heart" and "under the inspiration of grace," making it an act of communion with God.
G5215.portee: For the Christian, this entry reminds that sung praise is a fundamental spiritual discipline, not merely entertainment or decoration of worship. Hymns allow the Church to confess its faith together, to encourage one another, and to deepen the knowledge of God through its words. They reflect the joy of a community that celebrates its Lord together, uniting heart, spirit, and voice in common worship.

sens: To move from one place to another, generally on foot and without haste
To leave, to depart, to withdraw from a place
To head towards a specific destination
To die (euphemistic sense)
To progress, to advance in a direction or action
To obey an order, to carry out a command
G5217.detail:
1. The verb ὑπάγω (hupagō) primarily means to go or walk, but more slowly, more gently than the verb ἔρχομαι (erchomai): it is a quiet, steady movement. In John 3:8, the wind "goes" (ἂν θέλῃ, "where it wishes") without visible noise — the image is one of natural and peaceful progression.
2. The word also denotes the act of leaving or withdrawing: "let him go" (John 11:44), which means to allow the dead man to move out of the tomb freely, or "Get behind me, Satan" (Matthew 4:10), an order to depart.
3. When followed by a destination ("go to my vineyard," Matthew 21:28; "go work"), the verb expresses an intentional movement towards a specific place.
4. Euphemistically, "to go" can mean to die: "the Son of Man is going away" (Matthew 26:24) refers to Christ's death, as a departure to another world.
5. By extension, the verb is used for progress or an action that advances: "go and bear fruit" (John 15:16) literally means to move forward in your mission.
6. Finally, ὑπάγω is used as a term of obedience: "go, the demon has gone out" (Mark 7:29) commands the woman to leave, confident that she will obey and see the result.
G5217.origine: The word ὑπάγω is composed of ὑπό (hypo, "under") and ἄγω (agō, "to lead, to bring"). The basic image is that of leading someone to a place or under a direction, hence the meaning of "to lead slowly" or "to go gradually." Classical Greek uses it mainly in the present and imperfect tenses, rarely in the perfect or aorist. When the New Testament translates Hebrew texts, ὑπάγω often renders הָלַךְ (halak, "to go, to walk") or its derivatives, as in Exodus 14:21 (the wind that "goes" before Israel).
G5217.emploi: ὑπάγω appears 77 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (especially in John and Mark) and very rarely elsewhere (one occurrence in James 2:16, two in 1 John and Revelation). The verb is almost always used in the imperative (commands: "go work," Matthew 21:28; "go to the doctor," Mark 2:9) or in the present and imperfect (narrative of actions: "the demons went into the pigs," Matthew 8:32). John frequently uses it to express Christ's departure to His Father ("I am going to the Father," John 16:16) or the mystery of spiritual comings and goings ("you do not know where it comes from or where it goes," John 3:8). In Jesus, it is a word of authority: He commands to depart with assurance and peace ("go in peace," Mark 5:34), which implies that the one who obeys is healed, saved, or delivered. The context shows that it is a word of simple and peaceful movement, without urgency.
G5217.portee: For the Christian reader, ὑπάγω invites understanding obedience as a peaceful and trusting path: when Jesus says "go," it is not a harsh command, but a permission and a promise. The verb also reminds that spiritual life is a constant movement — going towards God, following His directives, advancing in the mission. Finally, the use of the word for Christ's departure to the Father (John 16:16) teaches that the believer's death in Christ is not an end, but a "going" into the presence of God.

sens: The act of listening to the one who commands and doing what he asks
The attitude of one who accepts the authority of another
Obedience to God and His commandments
Obedience to faith in Jesus Christ
The obedience of Christ Himself to God the Father
G5218.detail:
1. Obedience primarily means listening to someone who gives you an order and doing what he says. It is the opposite of disobedience or rebellion. This is clearly seen in Romans 6:16, where Paul asks: "By presenting yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one to whom you obey." Therefore, obedience is a form of voluntary slavery in service to the one to whom you obey.

2. Obedience is also the deep attitude of one who accepts the authority of another. It is not just executing an order mechanically, but recognizing the right to command of the one who speaks. In 1 Peter 1:2, the elect become "obedient" to the blood of Jesus Christ, which means they accept His authority intimately.

3. Very often in the New Testament, obedience primarily concerns God and His commandments. In 1 Peter 1:14, those who believe are called "children of obedience," meaning children who accept the will of God. Romans 16:19 praises the obedience of believers who keep themselves away from evil.

4. A particular form of obedience is that "to faith" or "in Jesus Christ." Romans 1:5 speaks of bringing all nations "to the obedience of faith" — this is the obedience that arises when one believes in Jesus and recognizes Him as Lord. In 2 Corinthians 10:5, Paul says we take "every thought captive to the obedience of Christ," meaning we submit all our reasoning to Jesus Christ.

5. The word also refers to the obedience of Christ Himself to His Father. In Hebrews 5:8, we are told that Christ "learned obedience through the things He suffered" — His entire life was a faithful obedience to God's plan, even to the cross. In Romans 5:19, "by the obedience of one" (Christ), all believers are justified.
G5218.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "hupakoúo" which literally means "to hear under," that is, "to listen to someone speaking from a position of authority." It is composed of "hupo" (under) and "akoúo" (to hear). The basic image is that of a servant listening to the orders of his master. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, similar words are found in the realm of "yes, I listen" — for example, the root "shema" which means "to hear" and "to obey." The Greek word appears only in the Bible and in ancient Christian writings: it is a quintessential biblical word.
G5218.emploi: The word "obedience" appears 13 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the first epistle of Peter. Paul uses it primarily to speak of the obedience owed to God and to Jesus Christ (Romans 1:5, 6:16, 16:19; 2 Corinthians 10:5). He also describes the obedience of Christ Himself to the Father as the foundation of our salvation (Romans 5:19). Peter, for his part, emphasizes the obedience of believers to the commandments of God and Christ (1 Peter 1:2, 1:14, 1:22). Paul also praises the obedience of the churches when they accept his apostolic instructions (2 Corinthians 7:15, Philemon 1:21). The word is always opposed to disobedience and sin: to obey God is to refuse to obey sin.
G5218.portee: Obedience reveals the very nature of the Christian life: it begins when one recognizes Jesus Christ as Lord (Romans 1:5) and consists of submitting one's entire life, thoughts, and actions to His will. It is not a crushing servitude, but the freely accepted acknowledgment of the authority of the one who loves us and has saved us. By contemplating the obedience of Christ Himself — the Son of God who obeys the Father unto death — we understand that obedience is not unworthy, but noble and salvific. It is the path to righteousness, sanctification, and eternal life.

sens: To listen, pay attention to a call or a sound
To respond to someone knocking at a door
To submit to an authority, follow an order
To accept and put into practice a message, a word
To place oneself under the authority of someone, to be submissive to them
G5219.detail:
1. The Greek word primarily means "to listen" — not just to hear noise, but to listen attentively, giving importance to what is heard. It is this attentive listening that prepares for obedience.
2. Scripture reports that the servant girl Rhoda "listened" (obeyed) to Peter's call knocking at the door (Acts 12:13): she heard and reacted to that call.
3. To obey means to submit to an authority, accept its command, and put it into practice. When the disciples are astonished to see that the wind and the sea obey Jesus (Matthew 8:27, Luke 8:25), they recognize an absolute authority over creation.
4. To obey the Gospel (Romans 10:16, 2 Thessalonians 1:8) means to actively receive and welcome the saving message — it is much more than a simple passive belief.
5. In human relationships, to obey is to voluntarily place oneself under the authority of another: children obey their parents (Ephesians 6:1), servants obey their masters (Colossians 3:22), believers obey the apostles (2 Thessalonians 3:14). It is to recognize the legitimacy of that authority and act accordingly.
G5219.origine: The Greek word ὑπακούω comes from ὑπό (under) and ἀκούω (to listen). The basic image is that of a person listening by placing themselves "under" the one who speaks — who places their listening under the authority of the one who speaks, which naturally leads to submission. In Hebrew, this word generally translates שָׁמַע (shamá, to listen) which carries the same richness: to truly listen is already to obey.
G5219.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Gospels. In the Gospels, it expresses the supernatural authority of Jesus: the elements obey Him (Matthew 8:27, Mark 4:41, Luke 8:25). Paul uses it to describe the moral obedience of believers: not to obey sin (Romans 6:12), to obey the truth (Romans 6:16-17), to obey the Gospel (Romans 10:16, 2 Thessalonians 1:8). In practical life exhortations, he describes the obedience of children, servants, and all believers to their legitimate authorities (Ephesians 6:1, 5, Colossians 3:20, 22). The epistle to the Hebrews speaks of the obedience of Jesus Himself (Hebrews 5:9).
G5219.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not just a mental adherence, but an active listening and practical obedience. To obey Jesus Christ is to recognize His authority in words and actions. It also invites the Christian to discern the legitimate authorities established by God (parents, masters, governments, Church) and to submit to them, not out of servile fear but out of recognition of their role. Joyful obedience to Christ and His word thus becomes the living sign of true listening.

sens: Subject to the authority of a man, particularly in marriage
Bound by the marriage bond to a living man
Legally dependent on a husband
G5220.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a woman "under" the authority of a man, as someone who is subordinate or dependent on another person. This is the literal meaning of the Greek word: "under a man." In Romans 7:2, Paul uses it to say that a married woman is legally bound to her husband as long as he lives.
2. In the marital bond, the married woman finds herself in a legal relationship with her husband. This legal connection is what Paul refers to when he states that a woman is "married" to a living man (Romans 7:2). This bond only exists if there is a living husband: upon the husband's death, this bond disappears and the woman is "released."
3. The word also emphasizes legal dependence: the married woman cannot remarry as long as her first husband is alive, because she is still bound by law to that husband. It is as much a legal concept as it is a relational reality.
G5220.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "hypo" (under) and "anèr" (man, husband). The image is therefore that of a woman placed under the authority of a man. It is a common construction in Greek to express submission or dependence. In Hebrew, the same idea was found in expressions like "under a husband" (אִישׁ תַּחַת), showing that this view of marriage was common in the biblical world.
G5220.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament: in Romans 7:2. Paul uses it to clarify the law of marriage while discussing the Christian's release from the law of Moses. He explains that just as a married woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives, so we have been "bound" to the law by our old nature, but released by the death of Christ. It is a legal and theological argument: the word designates the legal status of the woman in marriage, a status that is broken only by the death of the husband.
G5220.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that marriage is a serious legal bond, based on a commitment before God. It also shows that only death breaks this bond — a truth that Paul uses to teach how the death of Christ frees us from the condemnation of the law. Understanding the strength of this image helps to grasp the full depth of the Pauline analogy.

sens: To head towards someone to join or welcome them
To go to meet someone who is arriving
To walk towards an opponent in battle
G5221.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to set oneself in motion in the direction of a person to join or warmly welcome them. It is an active and intentional approach towards another. In Matthew 28:9, after the resurrection, Jesus "came to meet them" to greet the women who fell at his feet.
2. The word also denotes the action of going to meet someone who is arriving, often to receive them or bring them news. In John 4:51, the king's officer's servants "came to meet him" to announce that his son is alive — they leave their home to find him on the road.
3. In a warrior context, it means to march towards an enemy to confront them in battle. In Luke 14:31, a king examines whether he can "march to meet" an adversary who is coming to attack — it is a strategic question of direct combat.
G5221.origine: The Greek word is composed of ὑπό (hypo, "under") and ἀντάω (antaō, "to meet"). This composition creates the idea of going towards someone face-to-face, presenting oneself before them. The prefix intensifies the idea of a direct encounter. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it translates the Hebrew קָרָה (qārah, "to meet, to present oneself"), which has the same meaning of presenting oneself before someone or going to meet them.
G5221.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and once in Acts. It often describes the meeting between Jesus and people: the demon-possessed who "come to meet him" (Matthew 8:28, Mark 5:2, Luke 8:27), the women who rush to meet him after his resurrection (Matthew 28:9), Martha who goes to meet him before he arrives in Bethany (John 11:20), the crowd that goes out to meet him in Jerusalem (John 12:18). The word is also used for meetings between servants and master (John 4:51) or in military contexts (Luke 14:31). In all these cases, the idea is one of intentional and direct movement towards the other.
G5221.portee: This word expresses the initiative and willingness to meet, often highlighting the one who moves to welcome or confront. It reminds us that encounters with Jesus are never passive: people set out towards him, and sometimes it is Jesus himself who comes out to meet them — an image of mutual grace and personal commitment in faith.

sens: The action of going towards someone to receive or welcome them
The fact of being face to face with someone
G5222.detail: 1. It is the action of going out to meet someone, as one goes to greet an important person. In Matthew 8:34, the whole city comes out to meet Jesus to beg him to leave. In Matthew 25:1, the ten virgins go out to meet the bridegroom, awaiting his arrival. It is a gesture of honor or respect, marked by the movement of the one who goes towards the other. 2. More broadly, it is the situation of being face to face, being in direct presence of someone. In John 12:13, the crowd goes out to meet Jesus waving palm branches, which shows both the movement towards him and the meeting they seek to make with him.
G5222.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "hupantaô" which means "to go towards, to meet." The prefix "hupo" suggests a movement that goes from below to above or that goes to meet someone. The corresponding Hebrew word "qira" (קִרְאָה) in Judges 11:34 also describes a welcoming meeting, where Jephthah's daughter goes out to meet her father.
G5222.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Matthew and John, to describe the moment when people go out to meet Jesus or an important figure. In Matthew 8:34, it is the entire city that comes out to meet him urgently. In Matthew 25:1, the image of the virgins going to meet the bridegroom is one of active and vigilant waiting. In John 12:13, during the triumphal entry into Jerusalem, the crowd goes out to meet Jesus with honors. In all cases, the word marks an intentional and solemn movement towards an important meeting.
G5222.portee: This word reminds us that our relationship with Jesus is also a movement towards him: we go to meet him, we bring him out of our homes and hearts to welcome him eagerly. The image of the virgins going to meet the bridegroom also invites the believer to live in vigilant expectation and to prepare for the ultimate meeting with the Lord. It is a word of dynamism and active commitment in faith.

sens: What one possesses, one's heritage, material resources
Means of subsistence, what ensures existence
What has value and can be lost or abandoned
G5223.detail:
1. The word concretely designates everything a person possesses: their properties, money, material goods. In Acts 2:45, the early Christians "sold their properties and goods" to share the proceeds among all those in need: it is the entirety of what they possessed.
2. More broadly, it constitutes the wealth or substance of a person, what allows them to live. The word evokes the idea of what one "really has," in a stable manner.
3. In Hebrews 10:34, the text speaks of "better and lasting goods": the word emphasizes that earthly possessions, even significant ones, can be lost or taken away, unlike God's eternal realities.
G5223.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb huparchō, which means "to exist, to be present, to possess." It is essentially the noun formed from this verb: the things that "are" for someone, that they possess. In Hebrew, equivalent terms like rekhoush (wealth) or hon (substance, means) express the same idea of heritage and resources.
G5223.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 2:45, it describes the concrete action of the Christians in Jerusalem who, moved by the Holy Spirit, shared their possessions to support the poorer ones. In Hebrews 10:34, it contrasts earthly material goods with spiritual and eternal goods: persecuted believers accept the loss of their material possessions because they possess "better" ones in heaven. The word thus emphasizes the impermanence of material wealth.
G5223.portee: This word reminds Christians that their material possessions, however useful they may be here on earth, are not what truly matters. Acts 2 invites generosity and brotherly sharing; Hebrews 10 strengthens the persecuted believer by directing them toward true, eternal riches. It is an invitation to detach one's heart from temporary possessions and fix it on God.

sens: To own, enjoy goods, money, or objects
To exist, be present or available in a place
To be in a given state or condition
To belong to someone
G5225.detail:
1. To possess means to have as one's own, to be the owner of material goods. This is the most common meaning in the Gospels and Acts, where it refers to the money, lands, and livestock that someone holds. For example, Jesus tells the rich young man: "Sell what you possess, give it to the poor" (Matthew 19:21), or the early Christians did not claim that "their goods belonged to them alone" (Acts 4:32).

2. To exist or be present means that something is there, available, or visible in a place. Peter sees in a vision "all the quadrupeds and reptiles of the earth and the birds of the sky" that "were present" in a large sheet (Acts 10:12).

3. To be in a state or condition expresses a way of being, a lasting state. For example, Jesus says of those who refuse to follow him that they "have great possessions" (Luke 16:1 speaks of a rich man), or that someone "was a rich man" (Luke 23:50).

4. To belong to someone means to be the possession or property of a person. This is particularly seen in Paul: "No one said that their goods belonged to them alone" (Acts 4:32).
G5225.origine: The verb comes from the preposition ὑπό (under) and the verb ἄρχω (to begin, to be the origin of), hence the original meaning "to be underneath" or "to be ready." The word has gradually designated what is present, available, owned by someone — either as possession or as a lasting state. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, Greek translators used it to render הָיָה (to be), יֵשׁ (there is), and for terms designating material goods like רְכוּשׁ (property) or מִקְנֶה (livestock).
G5225.emploi: The verb appears 61 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels of Luke and Acts. It primarily expresses the material possession of goods, particularly among the rich or during distributions in Jerusalem: "Sell what you possess" (Luke 12:33), "No one said that their goods belonged to them alone" (Acts 4:32). It then signifies the existence or presence of something: animals "are found" in a vision (Acts 10:12). Finally, it describes a state or condition: "to be in need" (1 Corinthians 7:26) or "to be a rich man" (Luke 23:50). Paul also uses it theologically when speaking of Christ: he "existed in the form of God" (Philippians 2:6), expressing his divinity and glory before the incarnation.
G5225.portee: This word invites Christians to have a proper relationship with their goods: not a possessive attachment, but a willingness to share and give. The example of the early Christians, who did not claim ownership, shows the communal ideal that the Gospel calls for. When Jesus tells the rich young man to sell his possessions, he highlights that we are merely stewards of what we have. Finally, the same verb applied to Christ reveals his eternal existence and divine nature before his coming in the flesh.

sens: to withdraw, retreat
to bend, bow before someone
to accept the authority of another out of respect
G5226.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to withdraw or retreat in the face of a threat or pressure. It is the image of an army retreating.
2. The word then shifts to the idea of bending, bowing. This is not a shameful capitulation, but a conscious and voluntary submission to someone superior.
3. In Hebrews 13:17, Paul uses this verb in a moral and spiritual sense: "have deference for them" means to accept the authority of your spiritual leaders, to recognize their role, and to submit to their direction with respect. It is yielding not by force, but out of deference to those whom God has placed to guide you.
G5226.origine: The verb comes from the Greek composition ὑπό (under) and εἴκω (to yield, to make way). The basic image is that of someone who places themselves "under," who yields the place. This verb appears only once in the New Testament, making it a rare and solemn term, intentionally chosen by Paul to emphasize the seriousness of the respect due to spiritual leaders.
G5226.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 13:17, where Paul exhorts believers to obey their spiritual leaders and to have deference for them. The context shows that this submission is not forced, but motivated by respect for those who watch over souls. Paul adds that this attitude should be joyful, not begrudging, indicating a voluntary and conscious deference. The rarity of the term underscores its importance: it is a solemn call to honor those whom God has placed as guides.
G5226.portee: This word reminds believers that submission to spiritual authority is not humiliation, but a virtue. Yielding to the wisdom of those whom God has established as leaders means recognizing that we are not alone and that Christ also works through his servants. This voluntary deference fosters peace in relationships within the Christian community and allows leaders to serve with joy rather than burden.

sens: Placed face to face, across the path
That which opposes, that which obstructs
Contrary to, in conflict with
Hostile, enemy
G5227.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the spatial idea of something placed face to face, blocking the way. In Colossians 2:14, the ordinance of the law stood "condemning" — literally opposed — against us, like a written act that stood before us with its compelling force.
2. In a broader sense, "opposed" describes anything that creates an obstruction or resistance. It is what interposes, what creates an obstacle.
3. The main metaphorical usage is that of "contrary to" or "in conflict with," which goes against something or someone. The law was opposed to our salvation as long as it did not find its end in Christ.
4. In Hebrews 10:27, the word approaches the meaning of "enemy" or "rebel" — one who opposes God and His judgment, upon whom the fervor of fire falls.
G5227.origine: The word is composed of "hypo" (under, across) and "enantios" (facing, contrary). The starting image is that of a position that blocks the passage, standing in the way. It is a poetic and philosophical word used in classical Greek to speak of what opposes or comes into conflict. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it often renders Hebrew words like "enemy" or "adversary."
G5227.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Colossians 2:14, Paul uses it to describe the law and its ordinances that stood against us: they condemned us, opposed us, until Christ erased them by dying. In Hebrews 10:27, the substantival participle "the opposed" refers to the enemies of God, the rebels who refuse salvation, and upon whom judgment will fall. In both cases, the word emphasizes a radical hostility or contradiction.
G5227.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the Law itself, good as it is, opposed us as long as we were not in Christ — it condemned us. But Christ has removed this accusation. Conversely, one who rejects Christ becomes "the opposed" to God, the enemy, and faces judgment. It is a call to choose: to be with Christ, or against Him.

sens: In favor of someone, for their benefit, taking their side
To give or sacrifice one's life in exchange for the salvation of another
Because, for the reason that, due to
Regarding, concerning something or someone
Beyond, in excess of, more than
In place of, as a substitute for
G5228.detail:
1. To speak well of someone in their favor, to pray for them, to act in their interest: this is to take their side, to help them. For example, Jesus commands us to pray "for those who mistreat you" (Matthew 5:44), or Romans 8:31 asks: "If God is for us, who can be against us?", meaning that God is on our side.
2. To pay the price of another's life by giving one's own: this is the ultimate sacrifice. Jesus speaks of Himself as the good shepherd who "gives His life for the sheep" (John 10:11), and Paul says, "Christ loved us and gave Himself for us" (Romans 5:8).
3. The cause, the motive, the reason for doing something: we suffer "for the name of Jesus" (Acts 5:41) because it pleases God, or we give thanks "for" the comfort received (2 Corinthians 1:6).
4. The subject of conversation or thought: "as for Titus, he is our partner" (2 Corinthians 8:23) means "regarding Titus".
5. A quantity, force, or intensity that exceeds a limit: "beyond all that we ask" (Ephesians 3:20), or a suffering "more than we can bear" (2 Corinthians 1:8).
6. To replace someone else, to act or speak in their place: for example, those who are baptized "for the dead" (1 Corinthians 15:29) do so in their name, for them.
G5228.origine: This word comes from a Greek root meaning "above, over," a very simple initial image: what exceeds a limit, what is "on" or "beyond." The word has expanded in Greek to denote what is done "in favor of" someone, by extension of the idea of standing above or in front of someone to protect or help them. In composition, it enters into verbs like "to exceed" (ὑπερβάλλω), "to overcome" (ὑπερνικάω), or "to intercede" (ὑπερεντυγχάνω).
G5228.emploi: The word "for" (ὑπέρ) is one of the most frequent in the New Testament, used more than 140 times. It appears everywhere, especially in Paul's letters, where it primarily denotes the action of Jesus Christ dying in place of sinners and for their salvation (Romans 5:6-8, 1 Corinthians 15:3, 2 Corinthians 5:14-15). It also expresses intercessory prayer (Matthew 5:44, Romans 8:26-27) and suffering endured for the faith (Acts 9:16, 2 Thessalonians 1:5). The meaning of "beyond" or "more than" appears especially when comparing two things (Luke 16:8, Hebrews 4:12). Depending on the context, it can mean "because of," "regarding," or even "in place of" in some particular cases like 1 Corinthians 15:29.
G5228.portee: This word summarizes the grace of Christian salvation: Jesus gave His life "for us" (Romans 5:8), that is, in our place and for our benefit. Understanding all the meanings of "for" helps grasp how Redemption concerns us personally and how it engages our gratitude and intercessory prayer for others. It is a word that speaks of active love, self-giving, and a cause that transcends us.

sens: To rise above oneself, to swell with pride
To harm the dignity of another by placing oneself above them
To claim undue superiority
G5229.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a soul that swells, that rises like a body being lifted. It is pride in the physical sense of swelling, of puffing oneself up — Paul says he might risk becoming "puffed up" by the very excellence of the revelations he has received (2 Corinthians 12:7).
2. To boast is also to place oneself above others, to belittle them through one's presumption. This is why the Adversary, in the last days, will rise against all that is called God and will sit in the temple proclaiming himself god (2 Thessalonians 2:4): he poses as a rival to God par excellence.
3. This verb marks pretension and rebellion: it is the gesture of one who stands against an established order and claims to surpass or overturn it.
G5229.origine: The word comes from a composition: ὑπέρ (hyper, above, beyond) and αἴρω (airô, to lift, to raise, to remove). Literally, "to lift above" — the image is that of an elevation, an ascent that is neither natural nor legitimate. It is a rare compound word that reinforces the idea of excess and surpassing limits by its very structure.
G5229.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, always in the middle voice (reflexive form): the action returns to the one who is its author. In 2 Corinthians 12:7, Paul fears that the extraordinary mystical experience might cause him to boast — which shows that this risk threatens even the apostle. In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, it is the Adversary himself, the man of sin, who rises against God and claims to surpass Him: the word here emphasizes active and blasphemous rebellion. In both cases, it is an elevation that crosses a moral and spiritual limit.
G5229.portee: This word reminds the believer that pride is an inner threat, even for one who has experienced the highest graces: one must be careful to remain humble. It also warns us that human pretension to place oneself above God, or to refuse His authority, is the fundamental lie of sin — a rebellion that characterizes Satan himself and his agents. It is a call to sobriety and respect for the order that God has established.

sens: who has reached the age of puberty and can marry
who has lost the youth and freshness of adolescence
G5230.detail:
1. A nubile girl is one who has grown up and reached the age where she can marry and start a family. The Greek word ὑπέρακμος is formed from "akme" (the peak, the pinnacle of youth): it is exactly someone who has passed that peak of youth. In 1 Corinthians 7:36, Paul speaks of a girl whose father fears she may remain alone; Paul says that if he considers her to have reached this nubile age and wishes to establish her, she should be married.
2. The word also suggests that she has surpassed her prime youth, even though there is nothing pejorative in the expression: it is simply acknowledging that time passes and that a young girl's life is approaching its natural end.
G5230.origine: The word combines the prefix "hyper-" (beyond, above) and "akmos" (the peak, the flourishing of youth). The image is that of a flower that has passed its moment of full bloom: she is no longer at the height of her beauty, but she is entering a new phase. This root "akme" also appears in French in "acmé."
G5230.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Corinthians 7:36. Paul addresses the issue of marriage there, responding to fathers concerned for their unmarried daughters. The context is Paul's pastoral advice on celibacy and marriage: he wants to show that it is not a sin for a father to allow his nubile daughter to marry, although he considers celibacy more noble. The word does not reappear anywhere else in Scripture.
G5230.portee: This passage invites Christians to regard marriage with respect, not as a fall or a weakness, but as a natural and honorable state. For the young girls of Paul's time and for those today, it is a reminder that the natural desires to marry and start a family are not contrary to faith.

sens: higher spatial position
domination or superiority
the location of one thing in relation to another
G5231.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, the word designates what is situated higher in space: in Hebrews 9:5, the cherubim of glory are "above the ark," they physically overlook it.
2. It also expresses superiority of rank or power: Christ, in Ephesians 4:10, ascended "above all the heavens," which means He dominates, surpassing the entire celestial universe.
3. With abstract realities, it indicates that one thing exceeds or takes precedence over another: in Ephesians 1:21, Christ sits "above all rule, authority, power, and dignity," meaning that no power or force can equal His.
G5231.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "hyper" (above, beyond) and "ano" (upward, above). This combination reinforces the idea of height and superior position. In ancient Greek, this preposition is used with the genitive to mark what is "above" something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words like "al" (on) or "meál" (above).
G5231.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Pauline epistles or the letter to the Hebrews, and always to express the superiority of Christ. In Ephesians 1:21 and 4:10, Paul uses it to affirm that the Lord Jesus transcends all celestial and earthly powers, whether visible or invisible. In Hebrews 9:5, the term has a more descriptive scope: it situates the cherubim in the sanctuary. In all cases, it marks a relationship of height, whether spatial or hierarchical.
G5231.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer by reminding them that Jesus Christ is not subject to any power, that no cosmic authority can resist Him. It encourages trust in a Lord who dominates all realities, visible or hidden, and who continually fills the universe with His sovereign presence.

sens: Grow excessively, exceed any normal limit
Grow extraordinarily
Progress with surprising magnitude
G5232.detail:
1. The word describes a growth that exceeds what would normally be expected. In 2 Thessalonians 1:3, Paul says that the faith and love of the Thessalonians "increase more and more" — not simply that they progress, but that they grow in an exceptional way, going beyond ordinary measure. It is an overflowing growth.
2. The image is that of a plant or phenomenon that exceeds its natural limits, that continues to grow. Paul gives thanks to God because this extraordinary growth of faith and love shows the power of the Spirit at work in the Church.
G5232.origine: The word is composed of "hyper" (beyond, above) and "auxanō" (to grow, to increase). This composition reinforces the simple meaning of growth by adding the idea of surpassing, of excess. It is a word that expresses intensity and abundance rather than a mere increase.
G5232.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Thessalonians 1:3. Paul uses it to express his amazement at the spiritual progress of the Thessalonians: their faith and love do not just progress, they "increase more and more." This excessive and continuous growth is why Paul gives thanks to God without ceasing. The context shows that Paul seeks to encourage the Church by highlighting that its life of faith produces fruits that go well beyond the ordinary.
G5232.portee: This word reminds believers that true faith is not stagnant: it is called to grow, and this growth can be extraordinary when rooted in God. For Paul, seeing a Church whose love increases more and more is a visible sign of divine grace. It invites every Christian not to settle for ordinary piety, but to aspire to a spiritual growth that exceeds their own expectations.

sens: Exceed a set limit
Transgress a rule or commandment
Abuse someone by overstepping their rights
G5233.detail: 1. The word first evokes the physical image of crossing a boundary or threshold that one should not cross: going beyond what is permitted. 2. In a moral sense, it is to violate an established rule, to disobey what has been prescribed. 3. In the text of 1 Thessalonians 4:6, the verb refers to defrauding a brother, that is, abusing him in business by exceeding the limits of honesty and justice: "no one should defraud his brother or take advantage of him." It is committing an injustice by overstepping the rights of others.
G5233.origine: The word comes from the root "hyper" (beyond, above) and "bainō" (to walk, to go). The starting image is therefore that of someone walking beyond a limit, stepping over a boundary. This word belongs to the family of movement and action verbs. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it often translates the verb "avar" (עָבַר), which literally means "to pass" or "to cross" and is also used to express transgression.
G5233.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 4:6. Paul uses it to exhort Christians not to defraud their brothers in business transactions or affairs. The context shows that fraud is a form of transgression: it consists of crossing the line of honesty and justice by abusing one's neighbor. Paul reminds that the Lord "will punish all such things," which underscores the moral gravity of this transgression. The verb applies here to a violation of just relationships between Christian brothers.
G5233.portee: This word reminds Christians that justice towards one's neighbor does not only consist of avoiding obvious lies or theft, but also of respecting the limits of honesty in everyday business. To defraud is to exceed the line of what is just, and God watches over these seemingly small transgressions. It is a call to ordinary moral integrity in commercial and daily relationships.

sens: Beyond all measure
To an extreme degree
With excess or extravagance
G5234.detail:
1. This word expresses something that exceeds the ordinary limit, going beyond what is normally expected. In 2 Corinthians 11:23, Paul emphasizes that he has faced danger much more than other apostles, a danger that is "excessive," "beyond all measure."

2. It describes an intensity that surpasses everything that is usual or common. Paul wants his readers to understand that his trials are not ordinary, but extraordinary, radical.

3. The word highlights extravagance, excess — an insistence that something far exceeds the normal. It is the language of someone who says: "Not only much, but far beyond what one could imagine."
G5234.origine: The word comes from the verb "huperballō" which literally means "to throw beyond," "to exceed." The root "hyper" (beyond) and "ballō" (to throw) together paint the image of something that crosses a boundary. The adverb "huperballontōs" carries this idea to its adverbial degree, describing an action or state that exceeds measure. It is a relatively rare word in the New Testament, coined to express the idea of radical surpassing.
G5234.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Paul uses it to describe his exposure to danger as an apostle of Christ. In this highly personal and passionate context, Paul lists his sufferings — labors, beatings, imprisonments, dangers of death — and qualifies these dangers as "excessive," "well beyond all measure." It is an adverb that the apostle chooses to convey the extreme scope of his trials, not to boast, but to demonstrate his sincerity and dedication to the apostolic ministry.
G5234.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that authentic service to Christ may require a considerable price. Paul does not minimize his sufferings; on the contrary, he highlights them to show that the love of Christ has driven him to extraordinary risks. For the believer, this invites a radical honesty about the real cost of faithfulness — not to discourage, but to inspire deep gratitude and faith towards those who have given their lives to ministry.

sens: to exceed in excellence or intensity
to exceed measure or understanding
to transcend what can be known or limited
G5235.detail:
1. The verb first evokes the action of throwing something over or beyond a limit. Applied to spiritual qualities and realities, it means to surpass, to be superior in excellence. In 2 Corinthians 3:10, Paul states that the glory of the new covenant surpasses that of the old covenant: it surpasses it so much that the latter no longer shines in the eyes of believers.
2. The word also describes what exceeds ordinary measure, what is extraordinary in its scope or richness. In Ephesians 1:19, God's "infinite power" surpasses what the human mind can measure. In Ephesians 2:7, the richness of divine grace exceeds any imaginable limit.
3. More profoundly, it designates what transcends knowledge itself: in Ephesians 3:19, the love of Christ surpasses all knowledge, meaning that it goes beyond what can be conceptualized or understood by reason alone — one can experience and live it, but not fully grasp it.
G5235.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "hyper" (above, beyond) and "ballō" (to throw, to cast). The primary image is that of throwing something beyond a line or boundary. The compound is used metaphorically to express surpassing, excess, transcendence. In translations of the Greek Old Testament, it often conveys the Hebrew idea of excellence and superiority.
G5235.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Pauline epistles, particularly in Paul. In 2 Corinthians 3:10 and 9:14, he compares or qualifies the glory and grace of God: in the first case, the new covenant surpasses the old; in the second, the grace given to the Corinthians is described as "surpassing." In Ephesians, the word takes on a deeper and more contemplative significance: in 1:19 and 2:7, it describes divine power and richness as infinite, surpassing all measure; in 3:19, it culminates in affirming that the love of Christ surpasses knowledge itself. In all uses, it refers to divine realities or grace that exceed ordinary categories.
G5235.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God, His power, His grace, and His love cannot be confined within the limits of human understanding. Understanding that the love of Christ surpasses all knowledge frees us from the illusion that we can fully grasp it by reason alone, and calls us to experience it in faith and living relationship. It is a word of wonder at the greatness of God.

sens: Character of what exceeds, what is superior
Remarkable quality, superiority in a field
Abundance, profusion, extreme intensity
Excess, unmeasured extent
G5236.detail:
1. The word first designates what exceeds a limit, what goes beyond. That is why it can qualify what is excellent or eminent: Paul invites the Corinthians to aspire "to excellence" in gifts (1 Corinthians 12:31), meaning the best, the most eminent.
2. Excellence is a quality of what shines, what surpasses others. Paul speaks of the "excellence" of the revelations he has received (2 Corinthians 12:7), so much so that what has been revealed to him exceeds in greatness what one could imagine.
3. Often, the word means rather an unmeasured intensity, an extreme profusion. Paul describes the affliction that struck him in Asia as an "excessively" great burden, "beyond our strength" (2 Corinthians 1:8): the word paints a suffering that exceeds all normal measure.
4. In the same vein, the present afflictions produce a future glory "beyond all measure" (2 Corinthians 4:17), an infinite disproportion between the lightness of suffering and the heaviness of the reward. It is the idea of an excess that confounds.
G5236.origine: The word comes from "hyper" (beyond) and "ballō" (to throw): literally, to throw beyond. It is primarily an image of movement: what exceeds expected limits, which bursts forth beyond its measure. The image of throwing beyond gives rise to all meanings: that of excellence (what bursts forth in quality), that of profusion (what bursts forth in quantity), that of excess (what bursts forth without restraint).
G5236.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament, almost always in Paul. Sometimes it takes on a positive coloring: the excellence of spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:31), the excellence of revelations (2 Corinthians 12:7), the great power of God (2 Corinthians 4:7). Sometimes it emphasizes the idea of extreme intensity, often painful: the overwhelming burden in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8), the manifestation of sin at its "highest point" (Romans 7:13), the persecution led by Paul before his conversion, described as "outrageous" (Galatians 1:13). The nuance varies according to context: it can praise or highlight the excessive, but it always signifies a surpassing, a measurelessness.
G5236.portee: This word calls the Christian reader to a double contemplation. First, to recognize the excellence of God, the absolute superiority of what comes from Him — His gifts, His revelations, His power. Secondly, to understand that the disciple's suffering, however extreme it may be, weighs nothing compared to the glory that awaits him. It is a word that breaks all human proportion and directs us to the infinite greatness of God.

sens: Willfully ignoring something, not taking it into account
Tolerating without intervening for a time
Overlooking, leaving aside
G5237.detail:
1. This verb means to ignore or neglect something willfully, as if one were shutting their eyes to it. In Acts 17:30, Paul explains that God "shut His eyes to the times of ignorance": for a long time, God tolerated that the peoples ignored His will without immediately intervening to punish them.
2. It is not about forgetting or not seeing: it is rather about choosing not to react, to let it pass. God certainly saw the idolatry and ignorance of the ancient world, but He did not yet punish them, waiting for the time of judgment and repentance.
3. The word carries the idea of temporary tolerance, a suspension of judgment that will be followed by decisive intervention: after these times of patience, God "now commands all men everywhere to repent."
G5237.origine: The word is composed of "hyper" (beyond, above) and "eidos" (to see, sight). The basic image is that of a gaze that passes over something, that surpasses or circumvents it without stopping. It is a rare late Greek formation in biblical texts.
G5237.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:30, during Paul's speech to the Athenians at the Areopagus. Paul uses it to describe God's patience toward the pagan world during previous centuries: God did not immediately punish idolatry and religious ignorance, but tolerated them, waiting for the moment when He would call all peoples to repentance. This word thus expresses divine mercy toward the nations before the full revelation of Christ.
G5237.portee: This word reveals God's patience and grace toward humanity. It shows that God does not strike at the first failure: He waits, He tolerates, He gives time for repentance. But the "now" that follows also reminds us that this tolerance is not infinite, and that it leads to an urgent call to turn to Him. For the reader, it is an invitation to understand that God's waiting periods conceal a loving intention, not indifference.

sens: Further than, on the other side of
Further on, exceeding established limits
What surpasses, exceeds or transcends
G5238.detail:
1. In the simplest spatial sense: beyond marks what is on the other side of a boundary or geographical limit. In 2 Corinthians 10:16, Paul speaks of proclaiming the Gospel "beyond your region," meaning in areas that are beyond the territory already evangelized by his team.
2. The word also expresses the idea of exceeding established or agreed limits: to go beyond means not to be satisfied with what has been set or assigned. Paul specifies that he wants to preach "without boasting of what has been done in the limits assigned to others," emphasizing that he respects the boundaries of each person's work while seeking to expand his own field of action.
3. By extension, beyond can mean what exceeds, surpasses, or goes further than the ordinary measure — a figurative idea that enriches the spatial meaning.
G5238.origine: The Greek word ὑπερέκεινα (huperekeina) is formed from two elements: ὑπέρ (hyper), meaning "beyond, on the other side," and ἐκεῖνα (ekeina), meaning "over there, that side." This composition creates a prepositional phrase that reinforces the idea of distance and surpassing. The prefix ὑπέρ appears in many Greek words in the New Testament to express excess or crossing a limit.
G5238.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 10:16. Paul uses it in the context of his apostolic ministry: he explains his plan to extend the preaching of the Gospel beyond the territory where his team and he have already worked. This statement occurs in a defense of his apostleship against opponents who questioned his authority. The term highlights both a missionary ambition (to go further geographically) and a respect for the work of others (not to boast in fields assigned to others). It is a technical term in Pauline missionary vocabulary.
G5238.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the Lord's call to expand faith into yet un-evangelized territories, while respecting the work of other laborers.
