It invites us not to remain in comfort but to seek to push the boundaries of knowledge of Christ — a principle that should motivate every believer in their own sphere of influence, whatever it may be.

sens: to extend beyond what is appropriate
to make an excessive effort
to overstep one's own domain
G5239.detail:
1. To extend beyond what is appropriate: the word paints the image of something stretching, pulling beyond its natural bounds. Paul says he does not exceed his limits in preaching the Gospel up to Corinth, for it is indeed to Corinth that the Lord has sent him (2 Corinthians 10:14).
2. To make an excessive or presumptuous effort: it involves surpassing oneself, claiming more than what is assigned. Paul rejects the idea that he and his companions would exceed their strength or their charge to boast before the Corinthians.
3. To overstep one's own domain: each apostle has a field of work delineated by God; to exceed one's limits is to encroach on what belongs to another or to presume upon one's authority.
G5239.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "hyper" (beyond, over), "ek" (out of, from), and "teinō" (to stretch, to extend). The image is that of something being pulled or stretched too far, taking it out of its bounds. It is a rare word, formed to express the idea of excessive extension.
G5239.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 10:14. Paul uses it in his defense against those who criticized him in Corinth. He explains that he has not overstepped his apostolic authority: he has indeed gone as far as Corinth with the Gospel, which is his assigned field. He refuses the implicit reproach that his adversaries address to him: that he boasts of having evangelized beyond what was due to him. It is a technical term in his rhetoric of apostolicity and legitimate authority.
G5239.portee: This passage invites the Christian to recognize the limits of their own ministry and action. Everyone has a vocation, a particular field assigned by God; wisdom consists in remaining faithful to it without jealousy toward others, without wanting to conquer what does not belong to us. It is a lesson in humility and trust: God sets the boundaries, and we bless His work in other areas without envying them.

sens: To spill over the edge, to spread by exceeding a container
To greatly exceed a measure or expectation, to go beyond what is necessary
G5240.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of a liquid or substance that fills a container to the point of overflowing — the measure is so full that it spills out. In Luke 6:38, Jesus speaks of a measure of grain that is 'pressed down, shaken together, and running over': it is filled to the brim and overflows, illustrating the image of unrestrained generosity.
2. Figuratively, it expresses an abundant excess, something that surpasses the expected measure. The idea is one of superabundance: not only is the measure full, but it overflows as well. This indicates that God's blessing will be so great that it will exceed all expectations of the one who gives generously.
G5240.origine: The Greek word is formed from three elements: ὑπερ (hyper, 'above, over'), ἐκ (ek, 'out of'), and χύνω or χέω (chynō/chéō, 'to pour'). The basic image is that of pouring that flows upward and outward. It is a late and rare form of biblical vocabulary, created to vividly express this idea of complete overflow.
G5240.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:38. It is used in a discourse by Jesus where he invites his disciples to give generously, promising that God will give them a measure that overflows. The context is one of uncalculated generosity and disproportionate divine reward. The passive form of the verb ('it will be given to you') emphasizes that it is God's action that produces this overflow.
G5240.portee: This word reminds Christians of a key promise: generosity towards others never impoverishes. God gives 'a hundredfold', not by a simple equivalent return, but by an abundance that overflows. It is a call to trust in divine providence and to abandon the fear of lack. For the reader, this transforms the act of giving into an act of faith in the abundance of the Father.

sens: To intervene on behalf of someone before an authority
To plead the cause of another
To bring someone's needs before God in prayer
G5241.detail:
1. To intercede means to intervene, that is, to present oneself before someone more powerful to ask for something on behalf of another person. It is to speak for someone else, to carry their cause.
2. The word evokes the idea of pleading, that is, presenting a request with insistence and compassion. The one who intercedes takes upon themselves the needs of the other and brings them before the one who has the power to respond.
3. In terms of prayer, to intercede means to pray to God for someone else, to present their needs and sufferings to the Father. This is what the Holy Spirit does in Romans 8:26, where he intercedes for us 'with groanings that cannot be uttered' because we do not know how to pray as we ought.
G5241.origine: The word is composed of three parts: 'hyper' (beyond, for), 'en' (in, inside), and 'tugchanô' (to meet, to reach). The starting image is that of someone placing themselves 'inside' or 'in front of' an authority to 'go to meet' on behalf of another. It is thus a word of mediation and encounter.
G5241.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:26. Paul uses it to describe the mysterious action of the Holy Spirit who intercedes for weak believers, who do not know how to ask God for what they need. The Spirit comes to our aid in our weaknesses and carries our prayers before the Father in a form that human words cannot express. It is a hidden, intimate action, full of compassion.
G5241.portee: This word shows that we are never abandoned in our weakness and spiritual ignorance. The Holy Spirit himself takes care to present our true needs to God the Father, even when we cannot pray as we should. It is a promise of divine support in our moments of distress and uncertainty.

sens: To be placed higher, to physically dominate
To be superior in rank or authority
To excel, to prevail over something
To exceed in quality or value
That which is excellent, of surpassing worth
G5242.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word describes something that rises above something else, like something that exceeds or dominates (Exodus 26:13, where a part of the curtain is 'above').
2. When speaking of authority, it means to be invested with superior power: political authorities are 'superior' to those they govern (Romans 13:1, 1 Peter 2:13). It is the idea of rank, of hierarchical position.
3. When comparing people to one another, the word expresses humility: Paul exhorts the Philippians to consider others as 'above' themselves, that is, to esteem them more highly (Philippians 2:3).
4. For an abstract quality or reality, the verb means to exceed, to completely surpass: the peace of God 'surpasses' all human understanding, it infinitely exceeds it (Philippians 4:7).
5. Used as a noun ('excellence'), it designates that which has superior value: Paul renounces everything for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ, so much so that it surpasses him in value (Philippians 3:8).
G5242.origine: The word combines the prefix 'hyper' (above, over) and the verb 'echô' (to have, to hold). The basic image is thus one of holding something above something else. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this Greek verb often translates words meaning to dominate, to be strong, or to have the upper hand. The composition of the word emphasizes the idea of exceeding, surpassing, rising above.
G5242.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament. It is first used for civil authority: rulers are 'superior' to those who live under their authority (Romans 13:1, 1 Peter 2:13). It then describes humility in brotherly relationships: to regard others as 'above' oneself (Philippians 2:3). Finally, it expresses divine transcendence: the peace of God 'surpasses' our understanding (Philippians 4:7). When used as a noun, it becomes 'excellence' to qualify the supreme value of the knowledge of Christ (Philippians 3:8). The context varies, but the central idea remains that of what exceeds, dominates, or prevails.
G5242.portee: This word teaches the believer two lessons. First, it reminds them of the order established by God: established authorities deserve respect and submission. Second, it invites them to authentic humility: to consider others as superior to oneself. Finally, it confronts them with the infinite greatness of God and the knowledge of Christ, which surpasses all that man can desire or understand.

sens: Feeling of haughty superiority over others
Contemptuous disdain that leads to self-valorization
Humiliated refusal to accept one's place and limits before God
G5243.detail:
1. Pride is the feeling of believing oneself to be superior to others, looking down on them with disdain. It is arrogance, a high tone and demeanor that repels others. Jesus lists it among the vices that come from the evil heart (Mark 7:22).

2. It also involves the contempt expressed towards those deemed inferior: not wanting to look them in the face, treating them with indifference or harshness. The proud person inflates themselves and belittles others.

3. Finally, on a spiritual level, it is the humiliated refusal to accept being a creature, dependent and limited. Pride refuses to submit to God and to acknowledge one's own weaknesses—this is the root sin that diverts the heart from the truth.
G5243.origine: The Greek word comes from "hyper" (beyond, excessive) and "phainesthai" (to appear, to seem), literally "to appear beyond," meaning "to exceed the measure in appearance." It primarily translates in the Old Testament the Hebrew word "gaon" (greatness, magnificence), but when this word refers to a human attitude, it takes on the pejorative sense of proud arrogance. Pride is the illusion of one who appears greater than they are.
G5243.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 7:22. Jesus lists the twelve vices that come from the evil human heart: after murders, adulteries, and other crimes, He places pride among the serious moral defilements. The context shows that Jesus is not only speaking of an external fault but of an internal corruption. Pride is alongside deceit, lies, and envy—all these sins that arise when the heart turns away from God to fold in on itself.
G5243.portee: For the believer, recognizing pride within oneself is an essential step: it is the secret seed from which many other sins sprout. Jesus invites us to see it as a true corruption of the heart, not merely a bad manner. Guarding against pride means cultivating humility towards God and others—it allows grace to transform our relationships and our hearts.

sens: Who shows themselves above others, who places themselves higher
Who displays a haughty superiority, contempt for others
Who harbors an excessive pride in oneself
Who refuses to submit, to humble themselves before God
G5244.detail:
1. The word depicts one who stands above others, who exalts themselves. It is an attitude of one who believes themselves superior: they look down, they despise. In Luke 1:51, Mary sings that God "has scattered those who have proud thoughts in their hearts"—these thoughts that inflate the heart with fictitious greatness.

2. Pride manifests itself through an arrogant height, disdain: it is the attitude of one who refuses to recognize others as their equals. In Romans 1:30, Paul lists the "arrogant" among the worst vices, right after murders and ungodliness: it is a serious sin that corrupts human relationships.

3. It is the wrong conviction of being better, more worthy, more intelligent than others. In 2 Timothy 3:2, the "arrogant" appear in the list of selfish and corrupt characters of the last days: pride goes hand in hand with love of money and ingratitude.

4. Pride stands radically opposed to humility before God. In James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 (which quotes Proverbs 3:34), it is a spiritual battle: "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." The proud person closes themselves off to divine grace; only the humble receive it.
G5244.origine: The word combines two roots: "beyond" (ὑπέρ) and "to appear, to shine" (φαίνομαι). The starting image is therefore that of someone who "appears beyond," who shows themselves as elevated, shining of themselves beyond their true place. In Hebrew, this word translates several roots related to the sin of personal exaltation: rebellion (זֵד), haughty pride (גֵּאֶה), contemptuous laughter (לוּץ). It is always the attitude of one who places themselves above God and others.
G5244.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always to describe a serious flaw. In Paul (Romans 1:30 and 2 Timothy 3:2), it appears in the lists of sins that characterize fallen humanity, alongside murder, malice, and rebellion. In Peter and James, it is placed in direct contrast with humility: the proud oppose God and incur His resistance, while the humble receive His grace. The word thus retains a consistently negative sense in Scripture: it denotes not excellence, but a corruption of the heart.
G5244.portee: Pride is presented as one of the great obstacles to the grace of God. For the believer, this word targets the heart: it invites examination of whether we "show ourselves above," whether we despise, whether we refuse to humble ourselves. It reminds us that God "resists the proud" but "gives grace to the humble." It is an invitation to repentance and renunciation of self-exaltation.

sens: To be victorious in a decisive and total manner
To greatly surpass the opponent, exceeding mere victory
To triumph without being damaged or diminished by the battle
G5245.detail: 1. The word combines the idea of "beyond" (hyper-) and "to conquer" (nikaō). It is not just about winning or defeating one's opponent, but about greatly surpassing them, achieving a victory that goes beyond merely defeating the enemy. 2. The image is that of a warrior who not only defeats their adversaries but emerges from battle unscathed, strengthened rather than weakened. It is the total victory, one that leaves the victor intact and powerful. 3. In Romans 8:37, Paul uses this word to describe how Christians triumph over trials and sufferings: they not only survive or resist, but emerge "more than conquerors," transformed and strengthened by the love of Christ.
G5245.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ὑπέρ (hyper, "beyond, above") and the verb νικάω (nikaō, "to conquer"). This composition reinforces the simple meaning of the verb: it is not an ordinary victory, but a superior, complete victory that exceeds expectations. The prefix "beyond" transforms the ordinary victory into an absolute triumph.
G5245.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:37, in the context of the assurance of the Christian in the face of trials. Paul asserts that despite tribulations, persecutions, hunger, and nakedness mentioned in the previous verse, Christians are "more than conquerors" through the love of Christ. The choice of this strong term emphasizes that the victory of believers is not fragile or precarious, but solid and complete: it transcends difficulties without denying them.
G5245.portee: This word reminds the Christian in trial that it is not simply about surviving or enduring suffering, but about going through it while emerging strengthened and victorious. The believer's victory is not of this world, nor due to their own strength, but comes from the constant love of Christ. It is an invitation to trust: even in the most difficult spiritual battle, the Christian does not need to fear being crushed or facing definitive defeat.

sens: Excessively inflated word of vanity and pride
Arrogant and pretentious speech that seeks to impress
Puffed-up language, devoid of real substance
G5246.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of swelling, of excessive exaggeration: it is a word that claims more than it is worth, inflated like a balloon. In 2 Peter 2:18, false teachers entice young converts "with inflated words of vanity," meaning words that promise wonders but contain only hot air.
2. It is an arrogance that manifests through language: the arrogant speech of someone who wants to appear above others. In Jude 1:16, these men have "loud-mouthed words," revealing their pride and contempt for others.
3. The word emphasizes the contrast between pompous appearance and hollow reality: these inflated words are empty, they rest on nothing solid, unlike the Word of God which is true and enduring.
G5246.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "hyper" (beyond, excessive) and "ogkos" (weight, burden, volume). The basic image is that of swelling, excessive inflation — like an inflamed limb. It is a late word, primarily used in the time of the Apostles to describe speech that exceeds measure and swells with unfounded pride.
G5246.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, always to describe the language of false teachers and seducers. In 2 Peter 2:18, it characterizes the "inflated speeches" of false masters who lead young Christians astray using seductive but deceptive promises. In Jude 1:16, it qualifies the "loud-mouthed words" of those who criticize others and seek to elevate themselves. In both cases, the context is one of seduction and moral disorder: inflated speech always accompanies pride and deceit.
G5246.portee: This word warns the believer against the seduction of beautiful but empty language. It teaches us to discern between speech that inflates the ego (ours or others') and the true word that builds and strengthens faith. In the face of false teachers and the deceptive promises of the world, the Christian must learn to recognize the inflation beneath the elegant appearance of speech.

sens: that which exceeds, that which stands out above
excellence, preeminence of rank or quality
authority, dignity of a person placed above others
G5247.detail: 1. In its literal sense, the word denotes a projection or physical prominence: the peak that stands out — like the summit of a mountain rising above the rest. 2. Figuratively, it expresses excellence or preeminence: that which surpasses in quality or power. Paul refuses to preach the Gospel with a "superiority of speech or wisdom" (1 Corinthians 2:1), meaning by displaying an eloquence or human knowledge that would dominate his listeners. 3. The word also describes the authority or dignity that someone possesses due to their elevated position. To pray "for those who are in high positions" (1 Timothy 2:2) means to pray for authorities: those whose rank places them above others.
G5247.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to surpass, to dominate" (literally: "to hold above"). It first denotes what stands out from the crowd, what dominates by its position or nature. It is a term of excellence and preeminence used in Greek philosophy long before the New Testament.
G5247.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 2:1, Paul uses it to reject a style of preaching that would rely on rhetoric and worldly wisdom to impress or dominate his listeners; he prefers humility and simplicity. In 1 Timothy 2:2, it refers to political authority or power: "those who are in high positions" are magistrates and kings, those who hold a position of command. In both cases, it evokes a position of eminence or power.
G5247.portee: This word reminds us that the true power of the Christian message does not come from eloquence or outward appearance, but from the heart of the message itself. It also invites the Christian to respect and pray for those whom God has placed in authority, recognizing that their dignity comes from God.

sens: to exceed greatly in abundance
to be in extreme excess
to overflow with something
G5248.detail:
1. This verb expresses an abundance that exceeds mere quantity: not only having much, but having well beyond what is expected. In Romans 5:20, when Paul says that "grace has overflowed" where sin abounded, he means that grace does not merely equal sin; it infinitely surpasses it — it is an overflow that crushes the offense.
2. The verb can also describe a state of overflowing: in 2 Corinthians 7:4, Paul is "filled" with joy, overflowing with comfort despite his tribulations. It is a fullness that can no longer be contained, that spills over.
G5248.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "hyper" (over, beyond) and the verb "perisseuō" (to abound, to be in abundance), itself derived from "perissos" (which exceeds the measure, excessive). The addition of the prefix reinforces the idea: not simply to abound, but to surpass in abundance. It is a word often used in Greek to magnify or show an impressive accumulation.
G5248.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament, both times by Paul. In Romans 5:20, in the context of justification, it expresses how Christ's grace infinitely surpasses the power of sin — this is the heart of Paul's message of salvation. In 2 Corinthians 7:4, Paul uses it to express his emotional state: amid persecutions and sufferings, his joy does not lack; it overflows. In both cases, the word emphasizes an abundance that exceeds ordinary limits.
G5248.portee: This word reveals the overflowing nature of God's grace: it is never just sufficient, it overflows. For the Christian bearing burdens, it invites belief that God's comfort and joy surpass trials — not by denying suffering, but by the reality of a grace that remains greater and more present.

sens: to be present in very large quantity
to grow, multiply extraordinarily
to exceed greatly the measure or expectation
G5250.detail:
1. The word denotes a presence in great abundance, well beyond what is necessary: an overflow. In 1 Timothy 1:14, Paul speaks of the grace of the Lord that "has abounded excessively" toward him, like a wealth that overflows on all sides.
2. It also expresses a growth or multiplication that does not stop, that goes beyond the normal. Grace did not merely fill Paul; it spread over him with excessive generosity.
3. The image is one of surpassing: not only to suffice, but to surpass, exceed all expectation or measure — here the divine grace that does more than what is due or expected.
G5250.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "hyper" (beyond, excessively) and the verb "pleonazô" (to abound, to be in excess). This composition emphasizes the idea of an abundance that goes beyond ordinary abundance — an overabundance, a doubling. The Greek word translates the Hebrew idea of a grace that spreads generously, without measure.
G5250.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:14. Paul thanks the Lord for the faith and love that dwell in him, saying that "the grace of our Lord has abounded excessively with the faith and love that is in Christ Jesus." This passage celebrates God's extraordinary generosity toward a converted persecutor: grace not only forgave but flooded Paul with blessings beyond what he could have imagined.
G5250.portee: This word teaches us that divine grace never does just the minimum: it always exceeds our expectations and needs. Even when we feel unworthy or deeply sinful, God does not grant us just sufficient grace — he grants it to us with an abundance that overflows. For the Christian reader, it is a word of comfort: God's generosity toward us knows no bounds.

sens: Elevate someone above all, to the highest place
Give someone extraordinary dignity and honor
G5251.detail:
1. The word describes the action of elevating someone to a supreme position, incomparable to any other. It is an exaltation that exceeds all ordinary measure. In Philippians 2:9, God "sovereignly exalts" Jesus, meaning He places Him at a unique height, above all that exists.
2. This exaltation brings with it absolute honor and dignity. The word suggests not only a high position but the recognition of supreme value. When someone is exalted in this way, their unmatched excellence is proclaimed.
G5251.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "hyper" (beyond, above) and "ypsoō" (to elevate high). This composition reinforces the idea: it is to elevate beyond the normal, to raise to an excessive height. The root "ypsos" means height or altitude. The Greek here translates Hebrew verbs like "rûm" (to elevate, to exalt) and "'alâh" (to ascend), which belong to the biblical vocabulary of glory and divine royalty.
G5251.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:9. Paul uses it to describe what God did after the humiliation and death of Christ: He sovereignly exalted Him, giving Him a place of absolute honor. This exaltation is presented as the divine response to Christ's obedience and humility. The context shows that this exaltation is limitless and unparalleled in the universe.
G5251.portee: This word reveals the unique dignity of the risen Christ and His universal lordship. For the believer, recognizing that Jesus is sovereignly exalted by God Himself means placing Him first in their life and accepting His absolute authority. It is a call to worship and joyful submission to the glorified Lord.

G5252.fr: avoir une trop haute opinion de soi
sens: Have an exaggerated self-esteem, consider oneself superior to others
Disdain, treat someone or something with contempt
G5252.detail:
1. The word describes spiritual pride: this tendency to overestimate oneself, to believe oneself more important or more capable than others. Paul uses it in Romans 12:3 to warn against this natural inclination of the human heart: each one should evaluate their own worth "according to the measure of faith that God has given." It is a warning against religious self-sufficiency.
2. More broadly, the word can also mean to despise others, to consider them insignificant. This second nuance emphasizes how self-overestimation inevitably leads to disdain for others.
G5252.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: the prefix "hyper" (beyond, excessively) and "phroneō" (to have thoughts, wisdom). The basic image is of someone whose thoughts exceed reasonable measure. This construction is typical of Greek: it describes an exaggerated attitude of the mind or heart.
G5252.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 12:3. Paul uses it precisely in his call for humility within the Christian community. The apostle urges believers not to "have an exaggerated opinion of themselves" — which means to evaluate their faith and gifts at their true value, without exaggeration. This context shows that the danger addressed is particularly spiritual pride, the tendency to believe oneself a better Christian than one truly is.
G5252.portee: This word invites the reader to honesty towards oneself: to recognize that our abilities and merits are never what we imagine them to be. Pride is a trick of sin — it makes us exaggerate our strengths and diminish those of others. In Christ, true wisdom begins by knowing oneself as one truly is, what Paul calls here "putting on modest feelings." It is a call to lucid and joyful humility.

sens: Room located on the upper floor of a house
Room built on the flat roof of a dwelling
Meeting place or assembly of the early Christians
G5253.detail:
1. The upper room is a room located on the upper floor of a house, unlike the main rooms that are found on the ground floor. It is where the women of the house often lived in ancient Eastern culture.

2. More specifically, it refers to a room built on the flat roof of the house, a common practice in Palestine. This room allowed for an expansion of living space by utilizing the roof area (Acts 9:37).

3. In the New Testament, the upper room becomes the place where the apostles gather after the resurrection of Jesus. It is in Jerusalem that they assemble in this upper room to wait for the Spirit (Acts 1:13), and it is also where the apostle Paul preaches for a long time before a miracle occurs (Acts 20:8).
G5253.origine: The Greek word ὑπερῷον comes from ὑπέρ ("above") and literally means what is "above." The Hebrew word עֲלִיָּה (alijah) has the same meaning and signifies "ascent" or "that which is above." This root expresses the idea of rising or being situated at a height.
G5253.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, only in the book of Acts. It first designates the place where the apostles gather in Jerusalem after the Ascension (Acts 1:13). It also serves as a mortuary chamber for the body of Dorcas in Joppa (Acts 9:37, 39), a place where the body is kept in waiting and where Peter will perform the resurrection. Finally, Paul preaches there during his visit to Troas (Acts 20:8), and it is there that a young man named Eutychus falls from the window. In each case, the upper room is a private and elevated space, ideal for important gatherings of believers.
G5253.portee: The upper room reminds us that the Holy Spirit was received in an ordinary, intimate place, removed from the world. For the believer, it symbolizes the importance of prayer meetings and communal waiting, away from the tumult. It is also a sign that God acts in humble places and in the patient gatherings of disciples.

sens: Be subjected to a penalty, to a punishment
Endure a consequence, a judgment
G5254.detail:
1. The word designates the act of being subjected to a penalty or punishment. In Jude 7, Sodom and Gomorrah "suffer the penalty of eternal fire": they are exposed to divine judgment that consumes them. The image is of something that is "held under oneself," that one bears or endures to the end.
2. More broadly, it means to endure a consequence, a judgment that is inflicted upon us. The word implies a prior action (here, immorality and vices) that inevitably provokes this reaction (the punishment). The one who suffers is passive, struck by a force that surpasses them.
G5254.origine: The word combines the prefix "hypo" (under) and the verb "echein" (to hold, to have). The basic image is thus "to hold under oneself," "to support." In classical Greek, it could mean "to present oneself" or "to submit," but in biblical Greek, it takes on the meaning of undergoing a penalty or judgment. In Jude 7, it translates the Hebrew "sabel" (to bear a burden), which refers to the idea of enduring imposed suffering.
G5254.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 7. It describes the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah: these cities "suffer the penalty of eternal fire" as punishment for their unnatural sins. This unique usage places it in a context of divine judgment and definitive consequences. The use of the participle ("suffering") emphasizes the continuous and inevitable nature of the punishment.
G5254.portee: This word reminds us of a solemn truth: sin has consequences. Sodom and Gomorrah are not historical abstractions, but living examples of God's judgment. For the Christian reader, this serves as a warning: the vices we choose carry a price that we will have to pay. But it also speaks to those who fear they have committed the irreparable: God alone truly judges and condemns justly.

sens: One who listens and submits to an order, a word
One who submits to the authority of someone
Willing to follow commands without resistance
G5255.detail:
1. The word first paints the image of someone who listens attentively — who pays attention — and consequently obeys. This is why the fathers of Israel, who "did not want to obey" Moses (Acts 7:39), refused to hear his word and follow his authority.
2. To be obedient is to submit to the will of a person or authority. Saint Paul evaluates the Corinthians to see if they are "obedient in all things" (2 Corinthians 2:9), that is, if they accept his teaching and directives.
3. The word also describes an inner attitude of docility: a voluntary acceptance, without murmuring. Christ himself "became obedient to death" (Philippians 2:8), showing that authentic obedience is an act of free and total submission to the will of the Father.
G5255.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to listen" or "to hear" (ὑπό-, "under," and ἀκούω, "to hear"). Literally, it depicts one who listens "under" — who listens to the order and submits to it. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same semantic field links listening to obedience: it is the verb שׁמע (shama), "to hear" or "to obey," which expresses both at once. To obey is first to listen.
G5255.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to qualify an attitude towards authority. In Acts 7:39, it describes the refusal of the Israelites to listen to Moses; in 2 Corinthians 2:9, Paul uses it to test whether his readers submit to his apostolic authority; in Philippians 2:8, it is the obedience of Christ to the Father that becomes the ultimate model. In all cases, obedience is never passive or forced: it is a choice, a response to a word or command.
G5255.portee: The word invites the Christian to reflect on the deep meaning of obedience. It is not a mechanical submission, but an attentive listening and a free acceptance. The example of Christ (Philippians 2:8) shows that authentic obedience, even when difficult, is the path to glorification and peace. For the believer, being obedient to God and to His representatives means concretely listening to His word and putting it into practice.

sens: To serve as a rower on a ship
To help someone, to provide for their needs
To fulfill a mission in service to God
To render a service, assistance
G5256.detail:
1. In its original and proper sense: to serve as a rower on a ship, meaning to perform a subordinate but essential task that moves the boat forward. This concrete sense does not appear directly in the provided biblical usages.
2. To help someone by providing for their material needs or by rendering practical services. Paul tells the elders of Ephesus: "These hands provided for my needs and for those of the people who were with me" (Acts 20:34), showing that he supported himself and his companions through his work.
3. To fulfill a mission, to perform a function in service to God or according to His purpose. David "served the purpose of God in his own generation" (Acts 13:36): he accomplished the divine will during his life on earth.
4. To render service to someone, to be useful in a context of assistance or care. When Paul is in prison, he is "served" (Acts 24:23), meaning he is cared for and practically helped.
G5256.origine: The word comes from the noun "hypérétès" which literally designated the rower (one who rows under the orders of the pilot). The basic image is that of subordinate work, humble but indispensable: one rows to move the ship forward. In classical Greek, the word is always used in a figurative sense: to serve, to help, to fulfill a mission. The central notion is that of concrete and often modest help rendered to others.
G5256.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, only in the book of Acts (13:36, 20:34, 24:23). In all cases, it expresses practical help or the fulfillment of a function. In Acts 13:36, it describes David's service to the purpose of God: it is not about passivity, but about active participation in the divine will. In Acts 20:34 and 24:23, the word emphasizes the concrete, material help rendered to people: providing for their needs, serving them. The word always insists on practical involvement and often humble service, never on authority or prestige.
G5256.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that serving God is not an abstraction: it is to concretely fulfill His will. Like David, we are called to serve "the purpose of God" in our time. And just as Paul provided for his own needs and those of others, or as we help each other in prison, Christian service often involves material help and practical availability. It is the image of the rower: one does not see the one who rows, but without him, the ship goes nowhere.

sens: One who rows under the orders of a master, subordinate rower
Enforcement agent serving an authority: magistrate, court, police
Officer of the Jewish courts (Sanhedrin and synagogues)
Servant or assistant of a person of high rank
Minister of the Gospel or of Christ, one who serves the Word
G5257.detail:
1. The word first paints the ancient image of a rower located under the deck of a ship, executing the orders of the captain (the one who rows above). This image of subordination has given rise to the general sense of servant or assistant.
2. In civil contexts, it is one who executes the orders of a public authority: in Matthew 5:25, it is the officer of justice who imprisons on the judge's orders.
3. In passages relating to Jewish courts, these are the police agents of the Sanhedrin and synagogues, tasked with arresting or maintaining order: in John 7:32, the Pharisees send officers to seize Jesus; in John 18:22, an officer strikes Jesus in the praetorium.
4. Among the great, it is a servant or assistant: in John 18:36, the officers of Christ are His servants, distinct from His slaves.
5. In the New Testament, this word designates Christian ministers who serve the Word of God or Christ: Luke 1:2 speaks of officers of the Word (witnesses of Jesus' ministry); Acts 13:5 and 26:16 refer to those who assist the apostles and serve the Gospel.
G5257.origine: The Greek word comes from a very ancient image: ὑπό ("under") + ἐρέτης ("one who rows"), literally "rower from below." The man who rows at the bottom of the ship obeys the command; hence the word has acquired the general sense of "servant" or "auxiliary." The Hebrew עֶבֶד (ebed, slave, servant) often represents the semantic equivalent. The central notion is that of subordination and execution of orders.
G5257.emploi: The word appears 20 times in the New Testament, primarily in contexts of official authority and justice. It is first encountered with Roman magistrates (Matthew 5:25), then massively in the Passion narratives with the officers of the Sanhedrin and Pharisees who arrest or mistreat Jesus (John 7:32; 18:3, 22; Acts 5:22). Mark and Luke mention it during Peter's trial and denial. Gradually, the New Testament also applies it to Christian ministers: those who assist the apostles (Acts 13:5), those who serve Christ or the Gospel (Luke 1:2; 1 Corinthians 4:1). The meaning thus shifts from an agent of coercion to a voluntary servant of God.
G5257.portee: This word reminds us that every servant, whether an agent of civil justice or a minister of Christ, performs a function that places him under a higher authority. For the believer, it emphasizes that serving the Gospel is not a position of prestige but a joyful subordination to the Lord. Ministers of the Word are merely auxiliaries, instruments in service of God's message, not masters.

sens: Natural state of rest for the body and mind during which one sleeps
Drowsiness, numbness that gradually overtakes someone who struggles against sleep
State of inattention or spiritual insensitivity, negligence towards God
G5258.detail:
1. Sleep is the natural state in which the body rests and the mind dozes. It is a vital need that no man can reject for long. When Joseph receives the message from the angel, he 'awakens' from sleep to act (Matthew 1:24), showing that sleep is a state where consciousness fades away.
2. Drowsiness refers to that moment when sleep overtakes someone against their will, when the eyelids become 'heavy.' Peter and his companions struggle against the sleep that overwhelms them during the Transfiguration, before 'staying awake' and seeing the glory of Jesus (Luke 9:32). The young Eutychus in Acts 20:9 'falls into a deep sleep' during Paul's speech, defeated by the sleep that paralyzes him.
3. Figuratively, Paul speaks of 'sleep' as spiritual indifference: Christians must 'wake up' from sleep, meaning to emerge from torpor and inattention to the things of God (Romans 13:11). Jesus also uses the term to refer to 'death' as a sleep from which one can awaken (John 11:13).
G5258.origine: The Greek word hupnos comes from a root meaning 'to cover, to obscure': it describes the state where everything becomes obscured, where consciousness extinguishes. In Hebrew, it translates words like shéna (sleep) or halom (dream). Sleep is a powerful biblical image: it symbolizes not only physical rest but also the absence of awareness, and by extension, indifference or forgetfulness of eternal matters.
G5258.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in a concrete or obvious figurative sense. Three times it refers to actual physical sleep: Joseph awakens from sleep (Matthew 1:24), Peter and his companions are weighed down by sleep (Luke 9:32), Eutychus falls asleep during a speech (Acts 20:9). Once, Jesus speaks of sleep to refer to Lazarus's death in veiled terms (John 11:13). Finally, Paul uses it figuratively in Romans 13:11 to signify spiritual drowsiness, indifference towards God. The contrast between falling asleep and waking up structures the message: it is a call to vigilance.
G5258.portee: This word invites Christians to spiritual vigilance. Paul reminds us: it is not only the body that can fall asleep, but also the conscience, the heart, the faith. The sleep of the soul is the forgetfulness of God, the meaningless routine, the resignation in the face of passing time. The Gospel calls each person to 'wake up,' meaning to become aware of the proximity of salvation and to live in spiritual alertness.

sens: Marker of the agent acting in a passive action
Marker of the one who undergoes or endures the action
Indication of the cause or means that produces an effect
Position or situation of dependence and submission
Spatial position: under, beneath
Approximate moment or duration
G5259G.detail:
1. The most common meaning: the preposition introduces the one who performs the action when the verb is passive. For example, 'John will be hated by all' (Matthew 10:22) or 'he was tempted by Satan' (Mark 1:13). It is the agent responsible for what happens.
2. It also indicates the one who undergoes or endures the action: 'For me, it matters very little to be judged by you' (1 Corinthians 4:3) — the one who judges imposes their judgment on you.
3. It marks the cause or means: 'so that what the Lord had said through the prophet might be fulfilled' (Matthew 1:22) — the prophet is the channel through which God speaks.
4. It expresses submission and dependence: 'without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you' (Philippians 1:28) — the opponent has a hold on those who would be afraid.
5. Rarely, it indicates a spatial position: 'under' or 'beneath.'
6. It can indicate an approximate moment: 'around morning' (Acts 5:21) — around, approximately.
G5259G.origine: This preposition comes from ancient Greek and is constructed with three different cases depending on the context (genitive, dative, accusative). It fundamentally expresses the idea of what is 'beneath,' from which the image of the agent who controls or dominates the situation derives. In composition, it enters into words like 'obey' (literally 'to listen from beneath') or 'submit,' retaining this nuance of dependence and subordination.
G5259G.emploi: This preposition appears 165 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in passages where a passive verb indicates an action endured: the Lord acts through the prophet, John the Baptist baptizes by repentance, John is arrested by Herod, the disciples are recognized by the authorities. It is also used with neutral verbs or those having a passive sense (to suffer, to be controlled) to indicate what produces or causes the effect. It appears in all the Gospels and in Paul, notably in the letter to the Romans where it specifies God's action. A few uses show a spatial or temporal nuance, but the dominant usage remains that of the agent in the passive construction.
G5259G.portee: Understanding this preposition helps the reader discern who truly acts in a biblical event. When we read 'Jesus was tested by Satan' or 'we are saved by grace,' this preposition forces us to identify the true agent and the source of power. It also reminds us that we are never merely passive spectators: we are either under the domination, under the protection, or under the action of God or hostile forces, which invites vigilance and active faith.

sens: Below (place)
Near, in the hands of (proximity relationship)
By, on behalf of (the one who performs the action)
Subject to, under authority (dependence or authority)
Under the weight of (oppression, constraint)
Around, about (time)
G5259H.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: that which is placed beneath another thing, the lower space. A lamp placed under a bushel (Matthew 5:15): the light is hidden below. This is the basic image: something that is below, hidden, invisible.

2. The preposition also designates one who holds something or someone in hand: the doctors "in whose hands" the woman suffered (Mark 5:26) — she came to them, she depends on them. It is a relationship of proximity and practical dependence.

3. Very often in Paul, "under" expresses who performs the action, particularly after passive verbs. When it is said that something is done "by" someone, the Greek says "under" that person — they act upon it, they are the cause. For example, the Gentiles are "subject to the rulers" (Romans 13:1 in context): the rulers act upon them.

4. The sense of domination: being "under" an authority, a rule, or a power. Being "under the law" (Galatians 4:4) or "under the curse" (Galatians 3:10) means being subject to it, unable to escape it. It is the biblical image of one who lacks freedom.

5. Being crushed, overwhelmed "under" something: the idea of weight, burden. One who suffers is "under" oppression, a burden that presses down on them.

6. For time, "around, about": the day of Pentecost "about" the third hour (Acts 2:15 in context).
G5259H.origine: The Greek word ὑπό comes from an Indo-European root meaning "below." It retains this primary sense of lower position, which has gradually extended to the idea of subordination: the one who is below depends on the one who is above. In the Greek Old Testament, it is regularly found to translate the Hebrew that also expresses this subordination. In composition, it gives rise to many verbs: ὑποτάσσω ("to submit"), ὑπακούω ("to obey"), ὑποδέω ("to put on shoes"), all of which retain this nuance of inferiority, dependence, or hidden action.
G5259H.emploi: The preposition ὑπό appears forty times in the New Testament, especially in Paul. It combines with three different grammatical cases, producing three distinct nuances. With the genitive (the "case of the holder"), it expresses the agent of the action, particularly in passive constructions: Peter is recognized "by" the rulers (Acts 4:11). With the accusative (the "case of movement"), it describes the passage "under" something, submission to an authority or rule: being "under the law" or "under the curse." The Pauline context of Galatians clearly shows how the law was a guardian that kept believers "under" it before Christ. In Romans 6-7, "under sin" and "under the law" oppose the freedom in Christ. In Luke, the word remains more often spatial: a lamp "under" the bushel, a child "under" the arm. The constant idea is that of something or someone in a situation of inferiority, dependence, or subordination.
G5259H.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals the path to liberation. The Old Testament places believers "under" the law, "under" the curse, "under" sin: a condition of captivity. Jesus, born "under the law" (Galatians 4:4), removed this burden. Paul emphasizes: we are no longer "under" the law or sin, but "under grace." This word shows that the Christian life is not absolute independence, but a transition from one master to another, from sin to Christ. It is an invitation to reflect on who or what we are truly submitted to.

sens: Secretly incite someone to do wrong
Push someone to bear false witness or act against the truth
G5260.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the idea of "putting underneath" or "slipping under" — as if placing a malicious suggestion under someone's feet to make them fall. It is to secretly and intentionally incite, pushing someone to act wrongly or against their conscience. In Acts 6:11, the adversaries of Stephen "suborn" men: they secretly push them to bear false witness against him.
2. More specifically, to suborn means to corrupt someone to lie or commit a reprehensible act. The suborner acts through hidden persuasion or corruption, not by force. The false witnesses against Stephen were suborned — that is, they were paid or pushed to invent lies.
G5260.origine: The Greek word is composed of "hupo" (under) and "ballō" (to throw). The basic image is that of throwing or putting something underneath — hence the metaphorical idea of slipping a suggestion, temptation, or malicious instruction into someone's mind. This composition is typical of how Greek describes hidden or sneaky actions: what is done "underneath" escapes view.
G5260.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:11. It describes the action of Stephen's enemies who recruit false witnesses against him: not by forcing them, but by corrupting or persuading them to lie. It is an act of organized and intentional malice directed against a deacon of the early church who had pleased God through his wonders and signs.
G5260.portee: This word reminds the reader that the adversaries of the Gospel often act through indirect means: corruption, lies, false testimonies. It also shows how hostility toward believers can be organized and calculated. For the Christian, it is an invitation to remain vigilant against sneaky attacks and to seek God's protection in slander.

sens: A written model that one copies exactly
A behavior or conduct that serves as a model to imitate
G5261.detail:
1. The word first designates a sheet or outline left under the paper for a child to trace letters by following with their finger or pen — like a writing workbook where the letters are dotted. The basic image is that of a trace, an outline to be followed step by step.
2. By extension, it refers to any behavior or conduct that deserves to be imitated as is. In 1 Peter 2:21, Christ himself is presented as this "example": his suffering, patience, and love show Christians how they should walk — not as an abstract theory to understand, but as a trace to be followed concretely.
G5261.origine: The word comes from the verb "hypographô" which means "to trace under," "to write underneath": one traces letters or lines underneath (like under transparent paper), and the learner faithfully copies them above. This image of a traced model to follow naturally extends to any example worthy of imitation.
G5261.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:21. Peter uses it to explain why Christians suffer: Christ suffered for them and left them an example to follow. It is not an abstract theory, but a concrete and living model — one must walk in the very footsteps of Jesus, just as a child follows the traced lines in their workbook.
G5261.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not primarily a doctrine to memorize, but a path to follow by looking to Jesus. Just as an apprentice carefully copies a model, the Christian must examine the life of Christ — his patience in suffering, his love for his enemies — and reproduce it step by step. It is an invitation to practical imitation, not distant admiration.

sens: What is shown to imitate
What is observed to warn or learn a lesson
Copy or image that reproduces a heavenly model
G5262.detail:
1. The most common meaning: an action or conduct that someone proposes as a model to follow. Jesus washes the feet of his disciples and says to them, "I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you" (John 13:15). It is to imitate Jesus, who becomes a living example of humility and service.
2. The example as a warning: a situation or fate that is exhibited so that others may draw a negative lesson from it. The cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed by God, are given "as an example to those who would live ungodly" (2 Peter 2:6) — a spectacle of ruin that should provoke reflection. Similarly, the disobedience of the people in the desert remains an "example" of what should be avoided (Hebrews 4:11).
3. In the context of worship: the image or figure that reproduces an invisible reality. The objects of the tabernacle are "images" and shadows of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5 and 9:23) — what Moses saw on the mountain and reproduced according to the divine model. It is not the real thing, but its earthly representation.
G5262.origine: The word comes from the Greek "hypo" (under) and "deigma" (that which is shown): literally "that which is shown underneath" or "that which is presented to be imitated." The family includes "hypodeiknyumi" (to show, to demonstrate). In the Septuagint, it translates notably the Hebrew concept of a sign or visible lesson that God proposes to the people. It is a word used by later Greek writers in place of the more classical "paradeigma."
G5262.emploi: This word appears 6 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul (Hebrews), Peter, and in the Gospel of John. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, it designates either the cultic image (the tabernacle and its objects, copies of the heavenly model), or the warning from the Old Testament (the disobedience in the desert). In John, it is the living example that Jesus gives by washing feet. James uses it for the prophets, models of suffering. Peter uses it for Sodom, a sign of judgment. The word thus oscillates between imitation (model to reproduce) and lesson (warning to remember) or representation (copy of a heavenly prototype).
G5262.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds that the life of Jesus — his cross, his humility, his obedience — is the example to follow, not a mere theoretical lesson but a living model proposed for imitation. It also shows that the punishments of the Old Testament and the misfortunes of cities like Sodom are not random: they are "examples" that God gives to warn and instruct. Finally, it helps to understand that the rites of the tabernacle are not futile, but a pedagogical shadow of eternal realities: God speaks to man through visible images.

sens: To make visible, reveal to someone
To teach, convey knowledge or truth
To designate, indicate insistently
G5263.detail: 1. The primary meaning is simply to make visible, to render known or recognized. When John the Baptist asks the Pharisees, "Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" (Matthew 3:7, Luke 3:7), it is about showing, that is, making something known or revealing it. 2. The word also means to teach or make a truth learned: to convey knowledge clearly. This meaning is found when Jesus says, "I will show you whom he is like, everyone who comes to me" (Luke 6:47): it is about showing through teaching and example. 3. The word can also designate in a pointed and precise manner: when the Lord says, "I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name" (Acts 9:16), he clearly indicates to Paul what awaits him, with a didactic or revealing intention. The word emphasizes the direct and intentional nature of this communication.
G5263.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix ὑπο- (hypo, "under") and the verb δείκνυμι (deiknoumi, "to show, to indicate"). This combination first evokes the idea of showing by putting under the eyes, or of showing discreetly. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), this verb notably translates the Hebrew נָגַד (nagad) in its intensive form, which means "to make known, to declare": to say something in a solemn or explicit manner.
G5263.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament according to the provided witnesses, mainly in Luke and in Acts. John the Baptist uses it to challenge the crowds about the source of their fleeing from judgment (Matthew 3:7, Luke 3:7). Jesus uses it to announce a revelation or teaching: to show whom he is like (Luke 6:47), whom to fear (Luke 12:5). In Acts, the verb designates the action of God revealing to Paul his vocation of suffering (Acts 9:16) or that of Paul who manifests by example the true path of brotherly help (Acts 20:35). The word always emphasizes an act of revelation or significant direct teaching.
G5263.portee: This verb invites the believer to receive the teaching and revelation of God or his servants seriously: when God or Jesus shows, it is always for an important reason. It also reminds that the Christian faith is not an abstraction, but something that God makes visible, both through his words and through the concrete examples of those who follow him — like the example of generosity that Paul puts before his companions.

sens: To welcome someone into one's home, to offer hospitality
To treat someone kindly in one's own dwelling
To host, to lodge a guest
G5264.detail: 1. The primary meaning is to welcome someone into one's home to offer hospitality. Martha "receives" Jesus into her house (Luke 10:38), and Zacchaeus "receives" Jesus joyfully at his home (Luke 19:6): it is indeed about opening one's door and home to a visitor. 2. The word evokes a kind and generous welcome towards the guest: one "receives" him not coldly, but eagerly and joyfully, like Zacchaeus. 3. Rahab "receives" the messengers (James 2:25), meaning she welcomes them into her dwelling by hiding and protecting them. The verb emphasizes both hospitality and the commitment towards the one being received.
G5264.origine: The word is composed of "hupo" (under) and "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). The basic image is that of receiving someone "under" one's roof, that is, in one's personal and protected space. This preposition "under" reinforces the idea of intimate welcome and responsibility towards the guest.
G5264.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in the sense of welcoming someone into one's home. Luke uses it twice (10:38 and 19:6) to describe hospitality towards Jesus, in contexts where the welcome reveals the attitude of the heart: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, while Zacchaeus, transformed, receives him joyfully. James 2:25 uses it for Rahab who hides the spies in her home. In Acts 17:7, the verb takes on a different nuance ("to act"): it is a more general usage.
G5264.portee: This word reminds that receiving someone into one's home is not a trivial gesture: it is an act that engages the heart and reveals our values. Biblical hospitality is not mere politeness, but a generous and kind welcome that can transform the one who receives, as in the case of Zacchaeus. It also shows how Christians should welcome one another with the same warmth.

sens: To put sandals or shoes on one's feet
To be shod, to have sandals on one's feet
To prepare to walk or act (figuratively)
G5265.detail:
1. The verb properly means to put a sandal or shoe on someone or oneself. In Acts 12:8, the angel commands Peter: "Put on your belt and your sandals," a practical order for him to be ready to leave prison quickly.
2. The word also refers to the state of being shod, having shoes on one's feet. In Mark 6:9, Jesus advises his apostles to be "shod with sandals": this is a minimal provision for the journey, without seeking comfort.
3. In Ephesians 6:15, the verb takes on a figurative meaning: "and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace." Just as a warrior puts on his shoes for walking and fighting, the Christian "puts on" the Gospel to advance firmly in faith and face spiritual obstacles.
G5265.origine: The Greek word comes from the root déō (to bind, to tie) preceded by the prefix hypo (under). The primary image is that of the attachment under the foot, which binds the shoe to the foot of the walker. This root is found in other Greek words related to binding and tying. In Hebrew, the verb nāʿal (נָעַל, to close, to put on shoes) expresses a similar idea of putting on a shoe.
G5265.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always related to the action of preparing or equipping oneself. Twice, it is used in a literal and concrete sense: Acts 12:8 describes Peter receiving the order to put on his shoes to flee prison, and Mark 6:9 shows Jesus instructing his disciples to wear simple sandals. Once, in Ephesians 6:15, the verb is used figuratively in the description of the Christian's spiritual armor. In all cases, the verb suggests an action of preparation or disposition, either physical or spiritual.
G5265.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that the Christian faith is not passive. To be "shod" with the Gospel means to be ready to advance, to walk, to testify. It is also an invitation to simplicity and minimalism: the apostles took only the essentials. The verb invites the believer to consider how they spiritually prepare each day to face the journey of faith.

sens: Light shoe worn on the feet, secured by a strap
Mark of humility and service: untying the straps of a sandal is the work of a slave
Sign of dignity and social standing in a restoration narrative
G5266.detail:
1. The ancient sandal is a simple shoe, consisting of a sole attached to the foot by a strap — this is seen in the apostolic missions, where the disciples walk without sandals or wear them (Luke 10:4, Luke 15:22). It is the ordinary equipment of the traveler and the pilgrim.
2. The sandal has become symbolic of a servile task: untying someone else's strap was a gesture of a slave, so humble that John the Baptist declares himself unworthy to perform it for Jesus (Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16). This is why Jesus washes the feet of his disciples to signify his role of service.
3. In the parable of the prodigal son, the father orders sandals to be put on the restored son to reinstate his lost dignity (Luke 15:22): to wear sandals is to be treated honorably, not as a slave.
G5266.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to put under" (hypo- = under, deo = to bind): it literally refers to what is bound under the foot. In Hebrew, the term is *na'al* (נָעַל), which refers to the same image of the shod or uncovered foot. The ancient Mediterranean sandal was rudimentary: a simple sole attached by straps, which explains why untying it was a readily memorable and symbolically significant gesture.
G5266.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the Gospels and Acts, concentrated in four themes: 1) The sending of the disciples on mission, who must travel lightly and without sandals (Luke 10:4, Matthew 10:10), a way of saying they should not rely on material comfort; 2) The humility of John the Baptist and Jesus, who do not claim dignity (Matthew 3:11, Mark 1:7, Luke 3:16, John 1:27) — untying a sandal is too lowly a service for a prophet; 3) The restoration of the prodigal son (Luke 15:22), where the father puts sandals on the son as a sign of reintegration; 4) An Old Testament mention where Moses removes his sandals on holy ground (Acts 7:33).
G5266.portee: This word teaches a hierarchy of hearts: untying someone else's sandal is to recognize oneself as a humble servant. Jesus and John the Baptist refuse this honor to better signify their true greatness, which resides in God, not in themselves. For the believer, wearing sandals — or removing them — reminds us that we are never above the simplest task, and that there exists a nakedness of the heart more important than the clothing of the body.

sens: Stopped in speech, rendered silent
Obliged to acknowledge one's guilt, with no possible excuse
Subject to justice, liable to judgment
G5267.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a closed mouth, incapable of speaking or defending oneself: it is the forced silence of one who has nothing left to say. In Romans 3:19, Paul uses it to say that the Law makes "every mouth closed" before God, meaning that no one can argue or contest anymore.

2. To be closed means to be reduced to moral impotence: one can no longer claim innocence or justify one's actions. The Law exposes sin in such a way that everyone must acknowledge their guilt without being able to evade it.

3. In a legal sense, it means to be brought to justice, placed under the judgment of a court. Here, "being closed before God" means being rendered liable, responsible, and condemnable in the eyes of the supreme judge.
G5267.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: "hypo" (under) and "dike" (justice, trial). The image is that of someone placed "under judgment." It is a legal term that appears in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) to express guilt or subjection to divine justice.
G5267.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:19. Paul uses it in a decisive context: he concludes his argument that all human beings—Jews and Gentiles—are sinners and indebted before God. There is no escape: the Law closes all mouths and renders all men guilty (literally "recognized as guilty") before God. It is an absolute affirmation of the universality of sin.
G5267.portee: This word reminds Christians of a humbling and liberating truth: before God, none of us has a valid excuse. Our human justifications, our moralism, our self-sufficiency — all of this is silenced by the Law of God. But this forced silence is the path to grace: acknowledging our guilt without pretense opens our hands to receive the mercy of Christ, the only one who can justify us.

sens: Female of the donkey, work and pack animal
Figuratively, a stupid or insolent creature that opposes reason
G5268.detail:
1. The female donkey is the female of the donkey, a pack animal used for carrying loads or transportation. It is a humble and patient animal, commonly employed in the ancient Near East. Matthew 21:5 refers to it to describe the mount of the messianic king: the evangelist quotes the prophecy mentioning the colt of a female donkey, highlighting the humility of the Messiah who comes on an ordinary domestic creature, not on a war horse.
2. In contrast, the female donkey can also symbolize insolence or stupidity when it opposes wisdom. In 2 Peter 2:16, the female donkey of the prophet Balaam "speaking with a man's voice" represents a creature that God endowed with speech to stop the folly of a man: it becomes the divine spokesperson despite its animal nature, highlighting the absurdity of the prophet who ignores or despises God's message.
G5268.origine: The Greek word ὑποζύγιον (hupozugion) literally means "that which is under the yoke": it combines the prefix ὑπο (hupo, under) and ζυγός (zugos, yoke). This describes the animal subjected to work and the transport of loads. In ancient Greek, this term designates a pack animal or a beast of burden, and it regularly translates the Hebrew word חֲמוֹר (hamor, donkey). The word thus emphasizes the subordinate and laborious condition of the animal.
G5268.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 21:5, it is found in the citation of the messianic prophecy from Zechariah 9:9, where Jesus enters Jerusalem mounted on a colt, the foal of a female donkey — an image of poverty and radical humility that contrasts with worldly royal expectations. In 2 Peter 2:16, the female donkey of the prophet Balaam becomes a miraculous instrument of God's judgment: it rebukes Balaam by speaking in a human voice, illustrating the willful blindness of the prophet in the face of divine will. In both cases, the animal embodies a lesson: the Messiah comes without pomp, and even a mute beast can carry the word of God better than a proud man.
G5268.portee: These two uses invite the believer to revise their expectations: the Messiah manifests not through power and magnificence, but through humility and gentleness. The image of the female donkey also reminds us that God can use what seems weak or mute to confound our wisdom and bring us back to obedience. It is an invitation to recognize divine wisdom where carnal reason sees only poverty or absurdity.

sens: To wrap a cord or belt around something to hold or strengthen it
In navigation, to reinforce the hull of a ship by tightening cables around its length
G5269.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of wrapping a rope, band, or tie around an object to assemble, hold, or strengthen it: it is to tighten something from above, as one girds the loins with a belt. 2. In a maritime context, to gird a ship means to pass cables or chains under the hull and tighten them strongly to keep it together and prevent it from breaking under the shock of the waves. Acts 27:17 recounts how, during the storm threatening Paul's ship, the crew "used means of help to gird the ship": an emergency technical maneuver to prevent the boat from breaking apart.
G5269.origine: The verb is composed of the prefix "hypo" (under) and the verb "zōnnumi" (to gird, to surround). The basic image is that of a tie passed under something to enclose it. This Greek word appears only once in the New Testament, and it translates a well-attested naval practice in antiquity.
G5269.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:17, during the shipwreck of the vessel transporting Paul to Rome. It is a technical maritime term: it designates a concrete and precise rescue maneuver aimed at maintaining the structural integrity of a distressed vessel. Its unique and specialized use shows how Luke, the author of Acts, masters maritime vocabulary to recount this tumultuous journey authentically.
G5269.portee: This word reminds us that even in extreme peril — the storm threatening to destroy the ship — there are practical and courageous actions to take. For the Christian, it is a lesson of hope: in the face of adversity, one does not remain passive; one tightens, consolidates, and takes necessary measures. Paul himself urged the passengers to take courage, and it is by acting together that one holds firm.

sens: Position in space: below something, lower
Situation of dependence or submission
State of being covered or hidden
Domination or control exercised over someone
G5270.detail:
1. In a concrete spatial sense, "under" designates what is placed below another thing: the little dogs eat the crumbs "under" the table (Mark 7:28), the lamp is not placed "under" a bed (Luke 8:16). It is simply the position of one thing in relation to another in space.

2. The word is also used to signify the subjugation or control of one person over another: the enemies become the "footstool" of the Lord, an image that expresses their defeat and total submission (Matthew 22:44, Mark 12:36). This idea is found in Hebrews 2:8 with creatures placed "under" his feet.

3. Sometimes "under" expresses a hidden or concealed relationship: Nathanael was "under" the fig tree when Jesus saw him, which indicates a moment of intimacy or meditation (John 1:50).

4. In Revelation, "under" the altar are the souls of the martyrs (6:9), describing their rest in the presence of God, and it is "under" the throne that dwell the creatures who sing (5:3, 5:13, 12:1), expressing the order of creation where everything is subject to divine sovereignty.
G5270.origine: The Greek word ὑποκάτω is composed of ὑπό (hypo), which means "under" or "below," and κάτω (katō), "down" or "toward the bottom." This composition reinforces the idea of an inferior or low position. In the Greek Old Testament, this word regularly translates the Hebrew תַּחַת (tahath), which has exactly the same concrete and figurative meaning. The prefix ὑπό- in Greek often indicates the idea of subordination, whether spatial, legal, or moral.
G5270.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. Matthew, Mark, and Luke use it mostly in spatial and domestic contexts: placing an object under a table, under a bed. In John (1:50), it takes on a more mysterious hue by referring to Nathanael "under" the fig tree. The epistles and Revelation use this word in a more theological manner: Hebrews 2:8 cites the Psalm speaking of all things placed "under" the feet of the Son of Man; Revelation uses it to describe the celestial order where everything is "under" the throne of God or the altars. The Segond translates according to context: "under" for spatial, "footstool" for the image of domination, "dust" in the expression "dust of your feet."
G5270.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on two realities: first, the created order where each thing has its place, and nothing exists outside of divine arrangement. Secondly, it raises the question of submission and rest: everything is called to find its stability "under" the authority of Christ. For the believer, knowing that enemies are placed "under" the feet of the Lord is a source of confidence in God's final victory.

sens: To pretend, to falsely claim to be or have something
To play a role, to simulate an attitude or feeling that one does not have
G5271.detail:
1. To feign means to intentionally pretend, hiding one's true nature or intentions. In Luke 20:20, spies begin to observe Jesus while pretending to be righteous: they act like sincere devotees while in reality they want to trap him. It is a deliberate deception, a lie by appearance.
2. The word also evokes the idea of playing a role, like an actor on stage. It is to simulate, to perform a false identity or false feeling to deceive others or for a hidden reason.
G5271.origine: The Greek word ὑποκρίνω comes from ὑπό ('under') and the verb κρίνω ('to judge, to separate'). The primitive image is that of responding 'from underneath', secretly — hence it developed to mean responding on stage while playing a role (in ancient Greek theater). From there, it came to mean to feign, to conceal. The derived noun ὑποκριτής (hypocrite) has preserved and reinforced this notion of moral falseness.
G5271.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament in Luke 20:20. Jesus is confronted by adversaries who watch him while hiding their evil intentions under a guise of piety. It is a moment of tension: these spies are not honest; they are setting a trap. The context shows that feigning is a voluntary act of deception, linked to malicious motives (here, seeking to deliver Jesus to the authorities).
G5271.portee: This word reminds Christians of the danger of hypocrisy and falseness. Jesus encounters hypocrisy throughout his ministry and firmly denounces it. For the believer, it is an invitation to authenticity: not to play a role of piety, but to seek inner sincerity. The Bible calls to live in truth, not behind a mask.

sens: The act of playing a role, of presenting a false appearance
False moral or religious appearance; mask of piety worn to deceive
Behavior that contradicts one's true feelings or intentions
Malicious concealment; ruse intended to mislead others
G5272.detail: 1. The word originates from theater: it is the act of the actor who plays a role, who wears a mask to embody a character that is not himself (Luke 12:1). 2. In moral and religious life, hypocrisy is a false appearance of righteousness or piety: someone appears righteous in the eyes of others, but their heart is filled with malice (Matthew 23:28 speaks of those who 'appear righteous outwardly' but are 'full of hypocrisy' within). 3. It is also the lie of one who hides their true intentions: the Pharisees tempt Jesus not with a genuine question, but with hypocrisy, that is, by concealing their malice (Mark 12:15). 4. In social relationships, it is the ruse of one who pretends to believe or act sincerely while doing so only for appearances: in Antioch, even Barnabas was led astray by the hypocrisy of the Jews, that is, by their pretense (Galatians 2:13).
G5272.origine: The Greek word ὑπόκρισις (hupokrisis) comes from the verb ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrinomai, 'to respond', 'to play a role'), composed of ὑπό (hupo, 'under') and κρίνω (krino, 'to judge', 'to separate'). The image is of one who judges 'from underneath', who responds while hiding their true thoughts. In classical Greek and in Greek theater, the word designates the act of the actor playing a role, hence the meaning of 'feint' or 'dissimulation'. This Greek word often translates in the Greek Old Testament the concept of a false moral or religious appearance.
G5272.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the Gospels (Matthew and Mark) and in the epistles. Jesus denounces the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and the teachers of the law, who observe external rules while hiding a malicious heart (Matthew 23:28, Mark 12:15). In Luke 12:1, he warns his disciples against the 'leaven' of hypocrisy, that is, against this moral corruption that spreads like leaven in dough. Paul reproaches the Jews of Antioch for their hypocrisy: they no longer eat with the Gentiles for fear of the circumcised, thus hiding their true problem under a guise of piety (Galatians 2:13). False teachers can be recognized by their hypocrisy (1 Timothy 4:2), and the Christian must reject anything that approaches it (1 Peter 2:1).
G5272.portee: Hypocrisy is a major spiritual danger: it is not just an error or bad conduct, it is a lie that destroys the relationship with God and with others. Jesus denounces it with the greatest severity in those who claim to be religious but whose hearts are far from God. The Christian is called to seek sincerity and transparency: to say what they think, to live according to their convictions, and not to hide behind a false appearance of piety. It is a matter of heart veracity.

sens: One who plays a role, who pretends
One who claims a virtue they do not have
One who hides their true nature behind appearances
One who judges others while ignoring their own faults
G5273.detail:
1. The word originates from Greek theater: a hypocrite is an actor who plays a character, who wears a mask. It is someone who adopts an attitude that is not their own (Matthew 6:16: hypocrites make their faces unrecognizable to show that they are fasting).
2. In a moral sense, it is one who pretends to have qualities or piety that they do not truly possess, to impress others. In Matthew 6:2, hypocrites blow the trumpet when they give alms 'to be glorified by men'.
3. The hypocrite hides their true nature — their faults, their evil intentions — under a beautiful facade. Jesus in Matthew 23:27 compares the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees to 'whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly, but inside are full of dead men's bones'.
4. Paradoxically, the hypocrite harshly judges others while forgetting their own faults: in Matthew 7:5, Jesus invites to first remove the plank from one's own eye before seeing the speck in another's eye.
G5273.origine: The Greek word ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs) comes from the verb ὑποκρίνομαι (hypokrinomai), which literally means 'to respond under' or 'to play a role'. It is a compound of the prefix ὑπό (hupo, 'under') and the verb κρίνω (krino, 'to judge, to respond'). The term was used in theater to designate the actor who responds to other characters while playing a role. Transposed morally, it designates one who 'plays a role' in life, who simulates rather than being true.
G5273.emploi: The word appears 20 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew (14 occurrences) and less often in Mark and Luke. Jesus uses it primarily to denounce the religious leaders of his time — scribes, Pharisees, and some teachers of the law — who observed the external rules of piety (prayer, fasting, almsgiving) to be seen and admired, but neglected the justice and mercy of the heart (Matthew 23:23).
