The word also applies to those who judge others without examining their own guilt (Matthew 7:5), or who pretend to read the signs of the times without recognizing Jesus (Matthew 16:3). Jesus teaches that hypocrisy will ultimately be exposed: 'There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed' (Matthew 10:26, context of Luke 12:56).
G5273.portee: This word calls the believer to inner authenticity. True Christian faith does not consist of presenting a beautiful outward image, but aligning one's heart and actions. Jesus condemns hypocrisy because it distances one from God: it prefers the praise of men to divine approval, and it corrupts the community by providing a false model. Everyone is invited to ask themselves: where am I true, where am I pretending? The Holy Spirit frees from this tension by enabling a coherent life, based on grace rather than appearance.

sens: To carry or support from below
To receive, welcome
To interrupt, take the floor
To think, believe, imagine
G5274.detail:
1. To carry or support from below: the primary meaning of the word, an image of something that supports a weight or a person from below. This is how a cloud "took away" Jesus from the sight of the disciples by lifting Him up to heaven (Acts 1:9), as if it were supporting and carrying Him.

2. To receive, welcome: to give a warm welcome to someone, to admit them into one's fellowship. This is what Christians mean when they "welcome" workers of the Gospel into their homes (3 John 1:8).

3. To interrupt, take the floor: to jump into the conversation to take the place of the one who was speaking. Jesus "took the floor" in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30), inserting Himself into the dialogue that Simon had started.

4. To think, believe, imagine: to form an opinion in one's mind, to conclude mentally. Simon "thinks" that the one to whom the creditor forgave the most must love him more (Luke 7:43), or Paul asserts that Acts 2:15 warns the apostles: "These men are not drunk, as you suppose."
G5274.origine: The word combines the prefix ὑπό ("under, below") and λαμβάνω ("to take, seize"). The basic image is that of taking or supporting from below. It arises from daily life: one carries something by supporting it from below, just as one carries a child or a load. From there comes the idea of welcoming (receiving someone into one's home by supporting them), then that of "taking back," of inserting oneself into an exchange. Finally, the mental sense detaches itself: "to suppose" is to carry an idea in one's mind before verifying it.
G5274.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament. Luke uses it twice for acts of speech: to take the floor (Luke 10:30) and to form an opinion (Luke 7:43). Acts gives it more varied meanings: Jesus is carried up to heaven (Acts 1:9), the apostles are not drunk as one "supposes" (Acts 2:15). John, finally, uses it to speak of the hospitality that should be shown to the preachers of the Gospel (3 John 1:8). The word oscillates between the physical action of supporting and the mental action of judging or supposing.
G5274.portee: This word reminds the believer that our assumptions and hasty judgments are often just that: assumptions. When the disciples thought that Pentecost was drunkenness (Acts 2:15), they were mistaken. It also invites us to "welcome" generously those who work for the Gospel, supporting them as a faithful friend would. Finally, the divine support of Jesus by the cloud (Acts 1:9) symbolizes how God carries us and never abandons us.

sens: to survive, to be spared
to persist, to remain intact
G5275.detail:
1. To survive and be spared: the word describes one who remains alive after destruction or massacre. In Romans 11:3, the prophet Elijah says, "I alone am left," meaning that he escaped the massacre of the prophets perpetrated by the servants of Jezebel — he alone survived when all the others were killed.
2. To persist or remain: in a broader sense, it refers to what subsists or remains after other things have disappeared, like a remnant that persists in the face of destruction.
G5275.origine: The Greek word combines "hypo" (under) and "leipo" (to leave). It literally means "to leave under" or "to leave to subsist." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates roots that express the idea of remaining or surviving, such as "yatar" (to remain) or "shaar" (to subsist) — the common idea is that of the remnant that perseveres when the majority has disappeared.
G5275.emploi: This verb in the passive voice appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:3, where Paul cites Elijah's protest to God. Elijah complains of being "left alone" — the only survivor among the servants of God — while all the other prophets have been executed and the altars overturned. Paul uses it to show that at all times, a faithful remnant survives, even in the midst of Israel's general unfaithfulness. This key passage introduces the theology of the remnant in the letter to the Romans.
G5275.portee: This word reminds us that even in the darkest situations — massacre, persecution, widespread apostasy — God preserves a faithful remnant. It invites the reader to see that God's faithfulness does not depend on numbers or visibility, and that being "left alone" is never a definitive defeat in God's eyes.

sens: a container or pit dug under the grape press to collect the juice
the equipment for winemaking
the work or place of wine production
G5276.detail: 1. The word literally refers to the container or pit dug under the grape press, where the pressed grape juice flows and accumulates. In Mark 12:1, Jesus tells the parable of a man who plants a vineyard, surrounds it with a hedge, and "digs a winepress": this digging reveals the material work and investment of the owner in his vineyard, as it is a costly and permanent installation. 2. More broadly, the word can evoke all the equipment or system of winemaking, that is, not only the receiving pit but the entire system of transforming grapes into wine. 3. Sometimes, it is used figuratively to denote the intense work or pressure of God's judgment, particularly in the prophecies of the Old Testament (Joel 3:13, Zechariah 14:10), where the winepress becomes an image of divine vengeance that crushes nations.
G5276.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition "hypo" (under) and "lēnos" (the press or the winepress itself). Its basic image is therefore "that which is under the press," that is, the receiving container. This word translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew word "yeqeb," which designates both the vat where the grapes are crushed and the one where the juice flows. The family of the word "lēnos" goes back to the idea of digging and containing.
G5276.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 12:1, in the parable of the vineyard owner. Jesus lists the installations that the owner has made: he has planted, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress, and built a tower. Each detail shows the owner's investments and his trust in his vine workers. In the Old Testament (cited in the source definition), the word appears in prophetic visions to designate the winepress as the place of divine judgment, especially when the grapes represent the sinful nations crushed by God.
G5276.portee: This word invites the reader to notice the seriousness with which the vineyard owner invests in his property. In Mark 12:1, each detail — the hedge, the winepress, the tower — reveals the intention and trust of the master towards his servants. This prepares the heart to understand the tragedy of the end: despite this personal and costly investment, the vine workers will choose to reject the heir. For the believer, this shows how God has invested in His people with kindness, which makes the refusal to receive what He offers all the more serious.

sens: To abandon something when leaving, to leave it behind
G5277.detail: 1. To leave behind means not to take something with you when you go, or to abandon it on the spot. It is the image of a person who leaves a place and leaves a trace, an object, or a memory there. In 1 Peter 2:21, Jesus "leaves" us his example: he departs (to heaven after his resurrection), but he voluntarily, intentionally, leaves us his model of life and suffering for us to follow.
G5277.origine: The word comes from the prefix "hypo" (under, beneath) combined with a root that means "to leave" or "to abandon." It is closely related to other Greek words like "hypoleipô" (to leave aside, to omit), which share this idea of leaving something behind or beneath oneself. In the Greek Old Testament, this type of verb often translates the Hebrew idea of leaving or abandoning something.
G5277.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:21, in a passage where the apostle Peter exhorts persecuted Christians not to become discouraged. He explains that Jesus has voluntarily "left" (or transmitted to us) an example of patient and righteous suffering. It is a verb rich in pedagogical and spiritual meaning: what Jesus "leaves" is not a material object, but a model of life, a living lesson engraved in his redemptive work.
G5277.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus did not only save us through his death and resurrection, but that he also "left" us something more: a path to follow, a way to live and suffer with patience and righteousness. Recognizing this example means accepting that our faith is not only personal but also imitative, rooted in the model of Christ.

sens: to remain in a place, not to leave
to wait for something patiently
to endure with courage a trial, a suffering
to hold firm in faith until the end
G5278.detail:
1. The concrete meaning is simply to stay in one place: in Berea, Silas and Timothy "remained" when Paul had to leave (Acts 17:14). It is the idea of not moving, of staying put.

2. The word can also mean to wait for something: it is the patient waiting for a promise, as in Romans 8:24 where we wait for what we hope for.

3. The most frequent meaning in the New Testament is to endure, to bear a pain or trial with constancy. Love "bears all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7), meaning it holds firm in the face of any obstacle. Jesus himself "suffered" the cross (Hebrews 12:2), meaning he bore it steadfastly.

4. In a faith context, it is to persevere, that is, to remain faithful despite difficulties: "he who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22). It is an active patience that continues to believe and obey when everything would push to abandon.
G5278.origine: The word comes from two parts: "hypo" (under) and "menō" (to remain). The image is one of staying under, holding firm under the weight. In Hebrew, the same meaning is found with words like "qavah" (to wait firmly) or "yachal" (to hope). It is always the idea of holding firm, not yielding or fleeing in the face of pressure.
G5278.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. The four most common translations are: to persevere (5 times, particularly in Matthew 10:22 and 24:13 where it is about remaining faithful until the end despite persecutions), to bear (4 times, notably in 1 Corinthians 13:7 for love that endures all, and in Hebrews 12:2 for the cross that Jesus bore), to remain (2 times, in the concrete sense of not leaving), to suffer (2 times, in the sense of enduring a pain). The context reveals a nuance: in the Gospels, it is faithfulness under persecution; in the epistles, it is the patient endurance of the trials of the Christian life; in Hebrews, it is the ability to hold firm in faith.
G5278.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer who goes through difficulties or persecutions. It is not a resigned passivity, but an active firmness: to hold firm, not to abandon faith, to continue following Jesus despite the cost. The biblical promise is clear: he who perseveres will be saved (Matthew 10:22). It is a call to constancy and an assurance that God gives us the strength to endure.

sens: To bring back to memory something already known
To bring to mind a word or truth forgotten
To exhort someone by reminding them of what they should do or know
G5279.detail:
1. To bring back to memory something already known. It is to put before someone's eyes a dormant memory. Peter "remembered" the Lord's word at the moment of denial: what Jesus had said was engraved in him, but the moment of danger made him forget, and a simple look brings him back to reality (Luke 22:61).
2. To bring to mind a word or truth forgotten. The Holy Spirit "will remind you" of all that Jesus has taught: not to invent something new, but to shine anew on what has been heard, so that the disciple understands it again and more deeply (John 14:26).
3. To exhort someone by reminding them of what they should do or know. Timothy must "remind" the assembly of the truth it already knows, so that it remains alive and active. It is less about informing than about energizing memory and conscience: "remind them to be subject to rulers" (Titus 3:1).
G5279.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "hypo" (under) and "mimnesko" (I remember, I remind). The basic image is to place something "under" someone's consciousness so that they see it again. It is a reminder that passes through the deep layers of memory and conscience.
G5279.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. It describes three kinds of reminders. First, the involuntary reminder (Luke 22:61): a sign, an event brings to consciousness what had been repressed. Then, the divine reminder (John 14:26, Jude 1:5): the Holy Spirit or the voice of God restore the memory of his word and works. Finally, the pedagogical reminder (2 Timothy 2:14, Titus 3:1, 2 Peter 1:12, 3 John 1:10): a leader reminds believers of what they know but may forget, so that the truth acts in their lives.
G5279.portee: This word frees the Christian from the fear of a weakened memory. Even if we forget, the Lord through his Spirit brings us back to his word. It also invites church leaders to understand that their role is not to moralize, but to bring believers back to what they already know: grace, truth, the commandments of Christ. It is a ministry of faithfulness, not of novelty.

sens: Action of recalling to memory, making present to the mind
Thing or fact that is brought forward to remind of something
Exhortation intended to revive attention or vigilance
G5280.detail:
1. Remembrance is the action of bringing to mind what might be forgotten or set aside. Paul speaks of the "remembrance" of the sincere faith that first lived in Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5): he stirs up in him the memory of that faith to encourage him.
2. The word also refers to what serves as a reminder or memory aid — the concrete thing or fact that is evoked to maintain memory. This is why it can be used for an exhortation or a writing intended to revive attention.
3. In Peter's letters, remembrance becomes an active exhortation: the apostle seeks to "stir up by reminders" the pure understanding of believers (2 Peter 1:13; 3:1), not by teaching new truths, but by placing before their eyes what they already know, to keep them vigilant and faithful.
G5280.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb ὑπομιμνήσκω (to make remember, recall), composed of ὑπό (under, as a support) and μιμνήσκω (to remember). The basic image is that of placing something before the eyes of memory, or supporting memory as a prop. The prefix ὑπό gives a nuance of support and regular reminder, rather than a sudden or involuntary recollection. It is a typical word of the pastoral and exhortative register.
G5280.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, and exclusively in letters (2 Timothy and 2 Peter). In 2 Timothy 1:5, Paul uses it to speak of the living remembrance of an authentic faith passed down through a lineage. In 2 Peter 1:13 and 3:1, Peter describes his pastoral method: he writes not to teach new truths, but to maintain and revive through his letters the spiritual vigilance of his readers. The word thus embodies a form of ministry: the apostolate of reminder and exhortation, which combats distraction and forgetfulness.
G5280.portee: For today's Christian, this word reveals that faith is not a unique and static discovery, but a reality to be cultivated, revived, and transmitted. It also justifies the repeated exhortations of spiritual leaders: reminding is not reiterating, it is keeping alive what might fade away. And it shows that a solid faith, passed down by faithful witnesses (like Lois and Eunice), remains a source of encouragement throughout life.

sens: Act of staying, remaining in place
Ability to endure, to withstand a trial or suffering without wavering
Constant firmness in effort, faith, or obedience despite obstacles
Active constancy that firmly maintains a commitment or conviction
G5281.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of staying, remaining — a physical constancy that holds firm. This gives rise to the deeper meaning that runs throughout the New Testament.

2. The main idea is to endure, to withstand firmly a trial or suffering. In James 1:3, "the testing of your faith produces patience," which shows that we are not speaking of mere passive resignation, but of a strength that grows in the face of difficulties.

3. It is a firmness of soul in faith and obedience to God despite obstacles: in Luke 8:15, those who "hold fast to the word" and "bear fruit with perseverance" demonstrate how this quality expresses itself in spiritual life.

4. It is also an active constancy, a maintained commitment: in Romans 8:25, waiting "with perseverance" for what we have not yet received means holding firm in hope. In Revelation 2:2, "your perseverance" describes one who sustains his work and stands firm against evil. It is less about suffering patience than a strength that persists, endures without discouragement or turning away.
G5281.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to remain under" (hypo = under, monē = dwelling). The basic image is thus one of permanence, of holding: remaining in place despite pressures. Words of the same family all denote the act of supporting, enduring, remaining firm. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew *mikveh*, which evokes a confident expectation, a hope.
G5281.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles of Paul and in John. Paul uses it to describe a quality of the believer that grows through trials (Romans 5:3-4): tribulation produces endurance, which produces proven character, which produces hope. In Romans 8:25, waiting for the promise is done "with perseverance." James presents this quality as the fruit of the testing of faith (James 1:3-4): it must act fully until perfection. Revelation, in the midst of persecution, contrasts it with abandonment: "Blessed is the one who perseveres" (14:12). In 2 Timothy 3:10, Timothy must imitate Paul's perseverance. It is a virtue of those who hold firm despite obstacles, temptations, or sufferings.
G5281.portee: This notion invites the believer to see difficulties not as reasons to abandon, but as the ground where spiritual strength is forged. It states that true faith is measured by constancy, not by the absence of trials. For one who suffers or is tempted, it offers hope that holding firm actually grows faith itself. It is a word of courage for the disciple who commits long-term to God.

sens: To have an idea, an opinion about something without being certain
To suspect, to presume that something is true
To conjecture, to guess based on clues
G5282.detail:
1. To have an idea, an opinion about something without being certain: it is to form in one's mind a thought, a belief that is not based on certainty. In Acts 13:25, John says to the crowds: "I am not the one you think" — it is not a matter of assured knowledge, but of an impression, a hypothesis that the listeners have about his identity.
2. To suspect, to presume that something is true: it is to imagine, based on appearances or rumors, that something is the case. In Acts 25:18, Paul says that his accusers could prove nothing of what he supposed — that is, the accusations he feared or imagined would be brought against him.
3. To conjecture, to guess based on clues: it is to draw a probable conclusion from certain signs. In Acts 27:27, the sailors in a storm, hearing the sound of the waves and sensing changes in the sea, suspect that they are approaching land — a deduction made from fragmentary observations.
G5282.origine: The word comes from the composition of "hypo" (under, beneath) and "noéô" (to think, to have an idea). The image is that of a thought that remains beneath, not fully established: a provisional thought, an impression, rather than firm knowledge. It is a common Greek word that the translators of the Greek Old Testament used to translate the Hebrew verb "s'bar" (to estimate, to believe) in Daniel 7:25.
G5282.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, only in the book of Acts, always in the sense of forming an opinion without certainty. In Acts 13:25, John the Baptist uses it to say what the crowds suppose about him. In Acts 25:18, Paul uses it to speak of the accusations that were feared against him. In Acts 27:27, the sailors use it to describe their conjecture about approaching land. In all cases, the word carries the idea of a provisional thought, deduced from signs or rumors rather than established facts.
G5282.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of human opinion: what one supposes or suspects is never certainty. In Acts 13:25, it highlights the confusion of the crowds about the identity of the Messiah — they supposed, but John reveals the truth. It is an invitation to distinguish between what one believes to know by intuition or rumor, and what God reveals with clarity.

sens: A negative idea formed about someone without certainty
Unjustified distrust or doubt towards others
Suspicion that arises from pride and ignorance
G5283.detail:
1. Suspicion is a negative, vague idea without solid foundation that one forms about someone: thinking ill of them without having proof. It is to imagine or fear the worst. In 1 Timothy 6:4, Paul lists the spiritual consequences of pride and ignorance: from this arise envy, quarrels, slander, and also bad suspicions.
2. This word denotes chronic distrust, permanent doubt towards others — an attitude that poisons relationships and community. Suspicion is particularly dangerous in one who "knows nothing" and who, out of pride, judges others anyway.
G5283.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means "to think beneath" or "to suppose without certainty" (prefix hypo- = beneath, and root no- = to think). It is the idea of thinking about something without having examined the facts, allowing one's imagination to create accusations. In Hebrew, the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses similar words to denote malicious thoughts or suspicious ideas.
G5283.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:4. Paul uses it to describe the moral environment surrounding one who disputes over words and doctrines without love or wisdom. The context is clear: vain theological quarrels generate an atmosphere of mutual distrust, suspicion, and unfounded accusations. It is a vice that arises from spiritual pride and destroys communion.
G5283.portee: Suspicion reveals the heart of the one who harbors it. Jesus calls His disciples not to judge without certainty, not to suspect the worst of one another. In a local assembly, unfounded suspicions kill trust and brotherly love. Recognizing our unjustified suspicions is a step towards humility and reconciliation in Christ.

sens: To navigate while sheltered from the wind, along a land or an island on the side that protects from it
To pass near an island or a coast while staying close, rather than moving away from it
G5284.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of sailing by placing oneself under the wind of an island or a coast: the ship remains protected by this land from the violent winds blowing in front. It is a practical and necessary maneuver for a sailing boat when the winds are contrary. In Acts 27:4, during Paul's journey to Rome, the ship "sailed along the island of Cyprus" for this reason: the winds were contrary, so a sheltered route had to be followed.
2. More broadly, the word means to pass underneath, very close to an island or a coast, rather than going around it offshore. In Acts 27:7, the ship "passed under the island of Crete" while staying near the coast, despite the difficulty of the journey: it is a matter of direction and proximity to the land.
G5284.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "hypo" (under) and "pleō" (to sail, to navigate). The image is literal: to sail under, that is, on the sheltered side of a natural obstacle. No Hebrew word from the Old Testament has a direct equivalent, as this term is specific to Greek maritime vocabulary.
G5284.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in chapter 27 of Acts, during the long boat journey of the prisoner Paul to Rome. The context is one of difficult navigation: the winds are contrary, the ship must progress slowly and cautiously along the coasts and islands. The term reflects the practical and realistic knowledge of Mediterranean navigation of the time, and shows that Luke, the author of Acts, describes the details of a real maritime journey.
G5284.portee: This word shows us how early Christians, like Paul, face real obstacles and must adapt their route wisely. It also reminds us that divine Providence does not spare material difficulties but accompanies its servants even through a long and perilous crossing.

sens: To circulate air lightly and continuously
To produce a regular and easy breath (speaking of the wind)
To encourage someone with a discreet and benevolent presence
G5285.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of circulating air lightly, almost imperceptibly: a breath that is neither violent nor loud. In Acts 27:13, during Paul's shipwreck, "a gentle south wind" begins to blow softly after a flat calm — this breath deceives the sailors, who believe they can navigate at will.
2. Concretely, it is the wind itself that blows gently: a breeze that caresses rather than strikes. This regular and pleasant breath contrasts with the furious storms that ravage the ship elsewhere in the narrative.
3. The image can also evoke discreet encouragement, help that manifests without imposing its strength — like someone who blows behind another to help them move forward without pushing them.
G5285.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: the prefix "hypo" (under, lightly) and "pneō" (to blow, to breathe). This combination reinforces the idea of a tender and restrained breath rather than a powerful one. The prefix "hypo" often expresses the idea of something acting gently, from below, without violence — like a whisper beneath a strong word. The word "pneō" also recalls the Hebrew word for Spirit (ruach), which literally means "breath."
G5285.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:13, during the account of Paul's sea journey to Rome. At the moment of Paul's shipwreck, after several days of storm and flat calm that terrify the crew, "a gentle south wind" begins to blow softly. The sailors interpret this gentle and regular breath as a sign of improvement and believe they are masters of the situation — a fatal error, as the storm will return with greater force. This context shows how a light breath can be deceptive: pleasant and encouraging in appearance, but masking the true intentions of nature or God.
G5285.portee: This passage reminds believers that reassuring signs — an apparent improvement, a favorable wind, an unexpected respite — are not always reliable. The Christian pilgrimage often involves trials that resemble this maritime crossing: moments when one must resist false confidence and remain vigilant, turning to God rather than visible circumstances. This scene invites discernment between trusting one's own wisdom and surrendering to divine will.

sens: Small piece of furniture used as a footstool
Absolute domination of one person over their enemies
Complete submission of a lower authority to a higher authority
G5286.detail:
1. A footstool is a small piece of furniture or a platform on which one places their feet, usually positioned in front of a seat to facilitate access (James 2:3).
2. Figuratively, it refers to that on which one can walk, what is completely dominated: making one's enemies a footstool means to completely defeat them and submit them to one's power (Luke 20:43, Acts 2:35).
3. More broadly, it expresses total submission: when something is said to be God's footstool, it affirms that He completely dominates it, that He has absolute control over it (Acts 7:49: "the earth is my footstool").
G5286.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "hypo" (under) and "pous" (foot), literally meaning "that which is under the foot." It is an imaginative creation from Greek to express the idea of subordination and domination: what is under the foot has no power of resistance. The Hebrew Old Testament uses the Hebrew word "hadom" in the same royal imagery (Psalms 110:1, Isaiah 66:1).
G5286.emploi: This word appears seven times in the New Testament. One occurrence refers to a real object: in James 2:3, it is a true footstool, a small piece of furniture. But elsewhere, it is always an image: Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Hebrews use it to describe Christ's definitive victory over His enemies (Luke 20:43, Acts 2:35, Hebrews 1:13, 10:13), or God's absolute domination over all creation (Acts 7:49). All these metaphorical passages cite or are inspired by Psalms 110:1 or Isaiah 66:1, showing that it is a major image of royalty and the final victory of the Messiah.
G5286.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that Jesus' victory over evil is not a mere temporary defeat, but a total and irreversible submission: His enemies literally become His footstool. It is a promise of comfort for the persecuted believer: Christ already reigns over His adversaries, even if they still seem active. It also calls them to recognize that everything, in this world as in heaven, is ultimately subject to God's authority.

sens: foundation, base, support
substance, concrete reality
firm confidence, certainty
that which guarantees, title of ownership
G5287.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what supports something, its base or foundation — the idea of something that stands underneath and bears weight. This is why Paul uses it to speak of the firm confidence one can have in God: it is what supports our heart.
2. It can also mean the real substance of a thing, what makes it concrete and true — as opposed to what is merely appearance. The author of Hebrews uses it to say that Christ is the concrete and living imprint of the Father's person (Hebrews 1:3).
3. The most common meaning in the New Testament is assurance, unwavering confidence — a certainty that holds us firm. Hebrews 3:14 urges us to "hold firmly" to this assurance from the beginning, as if we were gripping the rock that holds us.
4. Faith, according to Hebrews 11:1, is the assurance (or title of ownership) of things hoped for — what guarantees us that what we do not see is nonetheless real and already belongs to us.
G5287.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that literally means "to stand underneath," "to support." This image of foundation or support explains all its meanings: what supports us, what truly exists (as opposed to appearance), and what makes us certain and confident. In ancient Greek Bible, it translates the Hebrew תִּקְוָה (hope, expectation) or מַצָּב (that which stands firm, solidity).
G5287.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and the author of Hebrews, to express unwavering confidence. Paul uses it twice in 2 Corinthians (9:4 and 11:17) to speak of the assurance he has to boast legitimately, or of the mutual confidence between the Churches. The author of Hebrews uses it three times: in 1:3 for the concrete reality of Christ as the reflection of the Father, in 3:14 to urge believers to keep their confidence, and in 11:1 to define faith itself as the assurance of invisible things. Its meaning nuances between personal confidence, concrete substance, and spiritual guarantee.
G5287.portee: This word reminds the believer that their faith is not an illusion or a mere fragile hope, but a solid assurance, anchored in God. When Hebrews 11:1 says that faith is the assurance of things hoped for, it is an invitation to receive what is not yet visible as already ours — a call to build one's life on the unshakeable foundation of God.

sens: To remove or hide something, to keep it away
To shy away, to retreat from a difficulty or duty
To abandon, to turn away from one's faith or commitment
G5288.detail:
1. The concrete meaning is to withdraw, hide, set aside: Paul tells his disciples that he has not hidden anything that was useful to them (Acts 20:20), as one withdraws or keeps a thing secret. It also means to leave aside, not to deliver.
2. To withdraw means to shy away, retreat, or hesitate in front of a task or person: in Antioch, Peter withdraws and keeps himself apart for fear of the circumcised who criticize his association with Gentiles (Galatians 2:12). It is a movement of retreat, excessive caution, or cowardice.
3. In the spiritual realm, to withdraw means to turn away, abandon: the righteous who withdraw from faith no longer have God's favor (Hebrews 10:38). It is a retreat, an apostasy, or a moral resignation in the face of conviction.
G5288.origine: The word comes from the root ὑπό "under" and στέλλω "to gather, fold, set in place." The basic image is that of folding something, bringing it back towards oneself or keeping it folded, hidden. The preposition ὑπό suggests a movement inward, a folding. In Hebrew, this verb often renders גּוּר ("to dwell, to reside, but also to fear, to keep away") or נָשָׂא פָּנִים ("to bear face," a turn of accent or respectful avoidance).
G5288.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul and Hebrews. In Paul (Acts 20, Galatians 2), it is a verb of concrete action: not hiding his preaching, withdrawing in front of a delicate social situation. The context in Galatians 2:12 shows Peter withdrawing for fear of judgment from others, abandoning his commitment to the Gentiles. In Hebrews 10:38, taking up Habakkuk 2:4, the word takes on an eschatological and moral tone: it is the believer who retreats in the face of persecution, who doubts. The word thus oscillates between physical or social withdrawal and internal abandonment.
G5288.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding faithfulness and spiritual courage. Peter in Antioch shows how human fear can lead us to abandon our convictions; Paul, on the contrary, claims transparency in his ministry. For the reader, "to withdraw" poses the question: do I have the courage to remain faithful in public, or do I retreat for fear of judgment? Hebrews applies it to perseverance in faith under threat.

sens: action of withdrawing, retreating
renunciation, cowardice in the face of commitment
loss of confidence, abandonment of faith
G5289.detail: 1. Withdrawal is primarily the action of retreating or backing away from a demand or danger: it is a backward movement, like that of a person who steps back from effort. 2. This withdrawal is also a renunciation, a cowardice: one who withdraws abandons their commitment due to a lack of courage (Hebrews 10:39). 3. In the context of Christian faith, it is the abandonment of trust in God and the refusal to persevere in obedience to Christ.
G5289.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ὑποστέλλω (hupostéllo), composed of ὑπό (hypo, "under") and στέλλω (stéllo, "send, post"). The image is that of a person who withdraws backward, who hides or evades. It is a word from the family of the verb "to retract" or "to retreat." This root expresses the idea of retreating from a responsibility or a trial.
G5289.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:39. The apostle uses it to contrast two attitudes in the face of persecution and trials: on one side, those who withdraw, who renounce their faith due to a lack of courage, and on the other, believers who persevere and maintain their trust. The context shows that this withdrawal is not a mere temporary failure, but a definitive abandonment of faith that leads to perdition.
G5289.portee: This word challenges the Christian reader regarding their faithfulness. It warns us that faith is not a passive adherence, but a commitment that requires courage and perseverance, especially in the face of difficulties and temptations to renounce. The contrast posed in Hebrews 10:39 invites us to choose: will we be among those who withdraw, or among those who keep the faith and reap salvation?

sens: To head back to a place one has left
To turn back, retrace one's steps
To revert to a previous state or condition
To restore or reinstate something
G5290.detail:
1. The most common meaning: to go somewhere again. Mary returned home after three months (Luke 1:56), the apostles returned to Jerusalem with joy after the resurrection (Luke 24:52). It is the physical movement of coming back to the starting point.
2. To turn back or retrace one's steps: John, during the missionary journey, returned to Jerusalem while Paul continued (Acts 13:13). The context shows a change of direction, a withdrawal.
3. To revert to a previous situation, especially after having received something: the Samaritan returned to Jesus to thank Him (Luke 17:15), which means to come back to a state of gratitude. A demon returns to its empty house and goes back to live there (Luke 11:24).
4. In some contexts, the word can also express restoration or reinstatement, as when someone returns to their normal state after healing (Luke 8:37, 39).
G5290.origine: The Greek word ὑποστρέφω (hupostrephō) is composed of ὑπό (hupo, "under," "again") and στρέφω (stréphō, "to turn"). The basic image is therefore to "turn again" or "to turn back to return." This verb primarily translates the Hebrew שׁוּב (shoub), which means "to return" and is one of the most important verbs in the Old Testament to express repentance and returning to God. The prefix ὑπό gives the Greek verb a nuance of renewed movement, of going back.
G5290.emploi: The verb appears 35 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke (about 20 occurrences) and in Acts (more than 10). Luke uses it for physical returns: the return of Jesus to Galilee after the temptations (Luke 4:14), the return of the apostles from mission (Luke 9:10), returns to Jerusalem after Easter (Luke 24:33, 52). In Acts, the verb describes the movements of the apostles during their journeys: returns to the starting point, turns in the road. With prepositions (εἰς, ἀπό, ἐκ), it specifies the direction: one returns "to" a place, one returns "from" elsewhere. The context is sometimes material and geographical, sometimes figurative of obedience or repentance.
G5290.portee: This verb reminds the believer that God often calls us to return — to Him first, but also to our responsibilities, to our first joy, to obedience. The return of the Samaritan to give thanks (Luke 17:15) shows that a true encounter with God brings us back to Him, filled with gratitude. The word invites us not to remain stagnant, but to turn again when the Lord guides us, with the assurance that returning to His presence brings joy.

sens: to place or lay something underneath
to prepare a bed or a resting place
to cover the ground by spreading things out
G5291.detail: 1. The verb literally means to place or arrange something underneath to prepare a surface or a path. In Luke 19:36, the crowds spread their garments on the road through which Jesus passes on His entry into Jerusalem, thus creating an improvised carpet in His honor. 2. The image also evokes preparing a bed by spreading fabrics or soft materials. 3. Figuratively, it can mean to prepare, organize, or set up a foundation for something.
G5291.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "hypo" (under) and the verb "strōnnumi" (to spread, to lay out). It is a later form of Greek that reinforces the idea of placing something underneath. The root "strōn" evokes the action of covering a surface by spreading materials.
G5291.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:36, during the account of Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem. In this context, it describes the action of the disciples and the crowds who spread their garments on the road to honor Jesus. This unique usage shows the specialized character of the term, used to describe a symbolic and festive gesture of respect towards the Lord.
G5291.portee: This act of spreading garments illustrates the honor given to Jesus and the triumphant welcome reserved for the Messiah. For the reader, it shows how the crowds recognize Jesus as king and prophet, and how faith is expressed through concrete and public acts of reverence. It is a lesson on how our worship of Christ should be visible and generous.

sens: The act of submitting to an authority, bending under the command of a superior
State of obedience to a law, requirement, or doctrine
Humble and respectful attitude of one who accepts the given order
G5292.detail:
1. Submission is primarily the act of yielding to the authority of a person or an established rule. Paul speaks of keeping children "in submission" (1 Timothy 3:4): it is to maintain them under order, under the respect of the father. It is a state of voluntary dependence.
2. It then designates concrete obedience to a particular requirement or doctrine. In Galatians 2:5, Paul resists the "demands" of false apostles: he refuses to bend to their claims. In 2 Corinthians 9:13, the "obedience" of Christians to the Gospel of Christ shows that they accept its truth and live under its authority.
3. Finally, submission is an inner attitude: that of the woman who "listens to instruction in silence, with complete submission" (1 Timothy 2:11), meaning she accepts the teaching with humility and respect, without resistance or murmuring.
G5292.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "hypo" (under) and "tagē" (order, arrangement, which comes from a verb meaning "to place, arrange"). It literally designates the act of being placed under, arranged under order. It is the state of one who submits. This word expresses a relationship of accepted order and hierarchy.
G5292.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Paul's epistles. In 2 Corinthians 9:13 and Galatians 2:5, it describes the obedience of Christians to the Gospel or the refusal to yield to false demands. In 1 Timothy 2:11 and 3:4, it occurs in passages concerning order in the Church and the family: the submission of women in the assembly, that of children in the home. In all these contexts, submission is never presented as humiliation, but as a principle of order and respect.
G5292.portee: This word reminds the believer that Christian freedom is not the absence of order, but the joyful acceptance of the authority of Christ and His Word. Submission to the truth of the Gospel is the fruit of the Spirit, not an external constraint. It is rooted in the recognition that God alone is master, and that by submitting to His order—in the Church, the family, responsibilities—we find wisdom and peace.

sens: to place or arrange under a military or administrative authority
to bring into obedience, to subjugate
to obey, to align oneself with someone's authority
to voluntarily submit to an order or direction
G5293.detail:
1. In a military or administrative sense: to place someone or something under the command or control of an authority. This is the basic image of the word, evoking a soldier placed under the orders of a leader.

2. To subjugate or bring into subjection: this means to make something dependent and obedient. For example, in 1 Corinthians 15:27, the apostle says that God has "put" all things under the feet of Christ—meaning He has placed them under His complete authority.

3. To obey or submit to someone: the passive or middle sense of the verb describes one who accepts this authority. In Romans 10:3, the Jews "did not submit" to the righteousness of God—meaning they refused to obey Him and trust His way.

4. To voluntarily submit, to choose obedience: this is the conscious and voluntary acceptance of an authority. In James 4:7, it is said: "Submit yourselves therefore to God"—this is a call to freely accept His authority. Similarly, in Ephesians 5:22, women are to be "submitted" to their husbands, not by constraint, but by a conscious choice to honor that order.
G5293.origine: The word comes from the Greek ὑπό (hypo), meaning "under", and τάσσω (tassō), meaning "to place, arrange in order". The original image is thus that of placing something or someone in a submissive position, under an established order. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word translates several verbs that express subjugation or obedience (such as דָבַר in causative mode, "to make obey"). In biblical Greek, the word retains this dual dimension: the action of submitting and the attitude of submitting.
G5293.emploi: The verb is used 32 times in the New Testament, notably in the epistles of Paul and Peter, and in the Epistle of James. It appears with two main meanings. First, in the active voice, it means "to put under the authority of", as in 1 Corinthians 15:27 where God submits all things under the feet of Christ. Secondly, in the middle or passive voice, it designates voluntary obedience or acceptance of authority: to submit to God (James 4:7), to the law (Romans 13:1), to a ruler, or in family relationships (wives and servants in Ephesians 5:22, Titus 2:9, 1 Peter 2:18). The nuance varies according to the context: sometimes it is a forced submission (like creation subjected to vanity in Romans 8:20), sometimes it is a free and obedient choice. In Luke 2:51, the child Jesus is presented as "submitted" to His parents, showing that submission is not disgraceful, but a virtue.
G5293.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the nature of authority and obedience. Unlike servile obedience, biblical "submission" is an act of freedom and trust towards God first, and then towards the authorities He has established. It is never blind, but based on the recognition that God is just and that His order is good. For the believer, submitting to God (rather than to one's own desires or the powers of the world) is the path to true freedom and peace.

sens: To place under, to lay underneath
To risk one's life, to expose it to danger
To present, to submit for consideration
G5294.detail:
1. The literal sense is to place something underneath, to lay it as a base: this is the image of the Greek word (hypo = under, tithēmi = to place). However, in the New Testament, this concrete sense does not appear directly.
2. In a figurative sense, "to expose one's neck" means to risk one's life, to put it in danger. In Romans 16:4, Paul praises Priscilla and Aquila who risked their necks for him: they accepted to lose their lives out of love for the Gospel.
3. In the middle voice (a form of the verb that marks rather an inner action or for oneself), the word means to propose, to submit for someone's reflection or decision. In 1 Timothy 4:6, Timothy exposes these things to the brothers: he presents them, proposes them, as if he were placing them before them for consideration.
G5294.origine: The word comes from hypo (under) and tithēmi (to place, to lay). The foundational image is that of something placed as a foundation or as a support point. The simple verb tithēmi is very common in Greek to mean "to place" or "to establish". The prefix "hypo" (under) nuances the meaning towards the idea of what is placed underneath, as a base, or figuratively, of what is exposed, brought forward. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb sûm (to place, to put).
G5294.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament. In Romans 16:4, it takes the meaning of risking one's life: Priscilla and Aquila have exposed their necks (that is, their lives, the neck symbolizing the life that can be lost) for Paul. This is an act of love and extreme courage. In 1 Timothy 4:6, in the middle voice, it means to present or expose: Timothy must expose these teachings to the brothers, proposing them as instructions to follow. The context is pedagogical: it is about transmitting faith and doctrine. Both uses show an action that puts something "forward" or "at stake."
G5294.portee: This word reminds the Christian of two important dimensions: complete devotion, even to the risk of life itself, to serve the Gospel (like Priscilla and Aquila); and the responsibility of the teacher to clearly present the Word of God to others. It is a call to generosity in service and faithfulness in teaching.

sens: To steer a ship by placing it under the wind of an island or obstacle
To shelter a boat from the wind by passing under the wind of land
G5295.detail: 1. The word refers to a navigation maneuver: positioning the boat so that an island or land serves as a shield against strong winds. In Acts 27:16, during the storm that takes Paul to Rome, the ship "sailed under the wind of the island of Clauda" — in other words, the sailors used this small island to protect themselves from the gusts, a tactical decision that allowed them to stabilize the boat and control the lifeboat. It is a technical term from ancient navigation, very precise.
G5295.origine: The word combines "hypo" (under, below) and "trechō" (to run, to move quickly). The image is of running — or rather sailing — under something, in this case under the wind of an island that breaks the force of the storm. It is a natural composition for maritime vocabulary: the boat "runs under" the protection of the land.
G5295.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 27:16, during Paul's shipwreck in the Mediterranean. The context is dramatic: the ship faced with a furious storm must find refuge. The experienced sailors react quickly by sailing under the wind of Clauda. This technical term reveals the precise knowledge of the author of Acts (probably Luke) regarding maritime navigation — a hint of historical authenticity.
G5295.portee: This word shows us how believers, even in extreme danger, can find refuge. Paul and his companions are saved by the wise action of the sailors seeking shelter: this illustrates how God often guides us through concrete and natural means. It is also a reminder that faith and human prudence go together — God does not magically remove danger, but does so through the intelligence and experience of those who act.

sens: A drawing, a sketch, or an outline that shows the main features of something
A pattern, a model to imitate or follow
A person or thing that serves as a model for others
What one should take as a guide in their faith life
G5296.detail:
1. The word comes from a verb meaning "to draw" or "to trace": it first evokes the idea of a sketch or diagram that presents the main contours of something, without all the details. It is like a sketch that shows the essential.
2. By extension, it designates a model, a pattern, or a formula that can be reused or imitated. In 2 Timothy 1:13, Paul speaks of the "pattern of sound words": it is like a form, a framework that Timothy must keep in mind and respect.
3. The word also applies to a person who embodies this model and becomes worthy of imitation. In 1 Timothy 1:16, Paul presents himself as an "example": his very life, the fact that Christ transformed him, should serve as a model for those considering believing in Jesus Christ.
4. In the life of faith, it is what we look to for how to live, how to believe, how to speak according to sound doctrine. It is a living guide or an established standard.
G5296.origine: The Greek word is composed of "hypo" (under, below) and "typos" (a blow, mark, imprint, figure). Literally, it is a "mark in relief", a sketched drawing where the essential traits are visible. The family of the word "typos" also gives us "example" (transliterated as "tupos"), which is more common in the New Testament. The verb from which our word comes literally means "to delineate" or "to trace the contours."
G5296.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible in Greek (1 Timothy 1:16 and 2 Timothy 1:13), always in Paul's epistles to Timothy. In 1 Timothy 1:16, Paul presents himself to Timothy as a living example: although he had persecuted Christians, Christ transformed him and showed him all his patience. This personal transformation is offered to those who want to believe in Jesus for eternal life. In 2 Timothy 1:13, Paul asks Timothy to "retain the pattern of sound words": it is a doctrinal framework, a schema of sound doctrine that Timothy received from Paul and must keep. In both cases, the word suggests something concrete and accessible, a model to keep in view.
G5296.portee: For a Christian, this word invites one to seek worthy models to imitate in faith: people transformed by Christ, whose lives testify to his power. It also reminds us that the received doctrine is not abstract, but must be kept as a model to follow. It is an exhortation not to invent a personal faith, but to rely on the example and teaching that have been given, while living them out concretely.

sens: To carry something heavy or difficult without yielding
To endure a trial, suffering, or temptation without giving up
To persevere in faith despite difficulties
G5297.detail:
1. The word comes from an image of a base: to carry something heavy from below, like a pillar that bears the weight of a building. It conveys the idea of holding firm under a load.
2. The Bible uses it to describe endurance in the face of temptations and sufferings. In 1 Corinthians 10:13, God assures that you will be able to bear the temptations that assail you, for they remain within your measure. In 2 Timothy 3:11, Paul recounts that he bore the persecutions and sufferings that struck him in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra.
3. This endurance is not passive: it is a grace, a strength given by God. In 1 Peter 2:19, Peter calls those who suffer unjustly to bear these afflictions for the love of God, which becomes a manifestation of faith.
G5297.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "hypo" (under) and "pherō" (to bear, to support). The original image is of holding firm under a weight, not collapsing. In Hebrew, this notion is often rendered by a word meaning "to lift" or "to bear" (nāsā'), which also expresses the idea of bearing a burden or moral load.
G5297.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always to speak of Christian endurance in the face of trials. In 1 Corinthians 10:13, it is the assurance that the believer can bear temptations. In 2 Timothy 3:11, Paul testifies to his own ability to endure persecutions. In 1 Peter 2:19, the context shows that it involves a moral and spiritual attitude: to bear unjust sufferings out of conscience toward God. Each time, the word denotes not a passive resignation, but an active firmness, sustained by divine grace.
G5297.portee: This word speaks to every believer going through trials, temptations, or injustices. It reminds us that God never allows a burden too heavy: he measures the trial to our strength and always provides a way out. To bear becomes an act of faith, a way to glorify God by remaining faithful despite difficulty.

sens: Leave a place to go elsewhere, move away
Step away from a crowd or situation to be alone or at peace
G5298.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical movement of leaving a place to go somewhere else. Jesus "withdrew to desolate places" (Luke 5:16): he departed from the presence of people to gain a deserted space. It is a simple and concrete change of location.

2. Beyond mere movement, the word emphasizes the idea of intentionally stepping away, creating distance. When Jesus "withdrew to a town" (Luke 9:10), it is not just about going elsewhere, but about removing himself from the crowd to find peace and solitude. The focus is on the solitude sought.
G5298.origine: The word is formed from two parts: "hypo" (under, behind) and "chōreō" (make space, move). The basic image is that of withdrawing "backward," yielding space, like someone who steps back. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb appears notably in Judges 20:37, where it also describes a movement of withdrawal.
G5298.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, both times in the Gospel of Luke, and both times referring to Jesus. In Luke 5:16, it illustrates Jesus' habit of regularly withdrawing to desolate places to pray, showing that his prayer life was a priority, even during his active ministry. In Luke 9:10, after the apostles returned from their mission, Jesus "withdrew" to a quiet place, emphasizing a moment of rest and private communion with his disciples. In both cases, the context is one of separation from the crowd for a spiritual purpose.
G5298.portee: This word reveals the importance of retreat and silence in Jesus' own life. For the Christian, it reminds us that withdrawing to pray, rest, or refocus is not a luxury, but a legitimate spiritual need. Jesus, despite his busyness and the crowds around him, took time to be alone with God. This invites the reader not to neglect their own moments of solitude with the Lord.

sens: Strike someone in the face, particularly under the eyes
Bother someone persistently and exhaustively
Treat one's body harshly through self-discipline
G5299.detail:
1. The word first evokes a blow received to the face, under the eyes, which leaves a visible mark — literally "give someone a black eye." This is the starting image: hitting someone repeatedly in the same spot.

2. Figuratively, it denotes the action of bothering someone, harassing them relentlessly with repeated requests. The widow in the parable "breaks the head" of the judge by continually coming before him (Luke 18:5): she exhausts him with her insistence, like a series of blows wear down a person.

3. The word also applies to the voluntary discipline of the body: Paul says he "disciplines" his body (1 Corinthians 9:27), meaning he subjects it to trials, "striking" it in a sense to master it and avoid becoming unfaithful to his calling.
G5299.origine: The word comes from the image of a blow struck "under the eye" (Greek ὑπό, under, and ὄψ, the eye or face). In Greek, this part of the face was particularly sensitive to blows. The verb originally meant to strike physically, then by extension to tire or test through repeated blows or continuous pressure. It is a word whose strength comes from its concrete physical image.
G5299.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 18:5, Jesus tells how the impatient widow "breaks the head" of the unjust judge with her repeated requests: it is the obsessive importunity that ultimately overcomes his inertia. In 1 Corinthians 9:27, Paul uses it to describe his own asceticism, the way he masters and subjects his body to trials: it is not about cruelty to oneself, but a consciously accepted discipline to remain faithful to his apostolic vocation. The word shifts from the sense of "harass" to the sense of "subdue" — in both cases, it conveys the idea of repeated pressure acting.
G5299.portee: This word teaches two lessons for the Christian. First, it shows that perseverance in prayer — even clumsy, even naive — ultimately gets heard: the widow "importunes" and obtains justice. Secondly, it reminds us that spiritual life requires a certain rigor: Paul disciplines his body not out of self-hatred, but so that his spirit remains free and obedient. It is a biblical image of self-control in view of the Kingdom.
